vulns.description: ### Summary  The keepalive timeout was not used during the initial portion of a request.  ### Impact  An attacker could keep an idle connection open indefinitely before sending any data.  ### Workaround  Use a reverse proxy (as recommended for all production deployments) with sensible keepalive limits.

### Summary  While reassembling a WebSocket frame that arrived across many small transport reads, the reader kept one `bytes` object per read with no bound on the count. The per-object overhead is many times larger than the payload bytes, so a frame delivered a few bytes at a time could use far more memory than `max_msg_size` allows.  ### Impact  An attacker could cause excessive memory use in a WebSocket server, or a malicious server against a client, by sending a frame in a large number of tiny segments.
### Summary  The Secure attribute was not being enforced for the shared cookie.  ### Impact  It may be possible to send a shared cookie marked Secure through an unencrypted request.

### Summary  The pure Python parser is vulnerable to an HTTP request smuggling attack.  ### Impact  If users are using the Python parser (`AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS`, or not a standard wheel installed), then an application may be vulnerable to a request smuggling attack.  ### Workaround  Switch to the default C parser.

### Summary  An attacker can exhaust file descriptors with specially crafted multipart requests.  ### Impact  If a handler uses `Request.post()`, it may be possible for an attacker to use an unlimited number of file descriptors, potentially resulting in resource exhaustion.

### Summary  A subdomain can remove the Host-Only flag from an existing cookie to a parent domain.  ### Impact  A user accessing untrusted subdomains could see their Host-Only protections stripped from cookies. Given most usecases won't reflect these cookies to a browser, the impact is limited.

### Summary  An overflow in Max-Age processing can skip closing a connection.  ### Impact  An attacker may be able to exhaust the connection pool temporarily, until garbage collection resolves the connections.

### Summary  An attacker sending an absolute-form request can spoof the scheme used.  ### Impact  If user code depends on the `Request.scheme` attribute for anything security related, an attacker may be able to circumvent this logic, tricking the application into thinking a connection is encrypted when it is not, or vice versa.  ### Workaround  A WAF rule to reject absolute-form requests (legitimate requests should only use this form for proxies).

### Impact Services using internationalized (non-ASCII) domain names are potentially vulnerable to TLS connections made from AnyIO's `connect_tcp()` or directly via `TLSStream.wrap()` where the connection has (through other means) been hijacked and redirected to a malicious server. The attacker would obtain a legitimate certificate using the IDNA 2003 encoded version of the domain name and offer it to the connecting client, making the certificate validate properly on the client's end.  ### Patches The vulnerability will be patched in v4.14.2.  ### Workarounds Encode host names via the `idna` package prior to connecting.

### Impact AnyIO starts process-pool workers with stderr connected to a pipe but never drains that pipe. The worker redirects stdin and stdout to /dev/null to protect its protocol, but does not redirect stderr even though the documentation says all three standard streams are redirected. Worker code that writes enough attacker-influenced data to stderr can fill the pipe, block before returning the stdout protocol response, and wedge the awaiting process-pool call.  Anyone who runs untrusted or faulty code that writes too much to `stderr` is at risk.  ### Patches This vulnerability will be patched in v4.14.2.  ### Workarounds Closing `sys.stderr` in the target function should at least prevent the deadlock.

Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them.   An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.  Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J` [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H` scores 7.1 (High).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.  Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`. - Sticky directories (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, any `1777` directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with `fs.protected_regular=2`). What remains is a planted non-empty `<db>-wal` (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. - Two kernel settings matter. `fs.protected_regular` (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in `/tmp`, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory. - Platform and route. The `/proc/self/fd` redirect is Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (`-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without `/proc`) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after it. Windows does not take this path. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename an entry in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_connect_through_descriptor` builds `/proc/self/fd/<n>` and hands it to `sqlite3.connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L982-L1001). The assumption is the [comment at line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), "Descriptor paths reopen the validated inode" (an inode is the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). SQLite first reads the file it opened at [`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, line 816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). The check in [`_raise_if_database_replaced` at line 836](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L836) runs only after `BEGIN`. Both [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect the descriptor, not the file SQLite is on. The one-level hard link of the macOS route is [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029).  ## Introduced  The `/proc/self/fd` redirect came with `4d45e83` ("Merge commit from fork", the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56), first released in **4.0.9** (verified: `git tag --contains 4d45e83` gives 4.0.9); 4.0.8 does not have it. The side-file variants are older. They reproduce on `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)"), first released in **3.20.4** (verified), which passed the lock path straight to `sqlite3.connect`.  ## Mechanism  On Linux the lock opens the database with `O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`. It checks through the descriptor that the file is a regular file and not a WAL database. It then calls `sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/<n>")` and expects SQLite to reopen the validated inode. SQLite does not open that name. It runs `readlink()` on it, which yields the path string the kernel reports for the descriptor at that moment, and opens that string by path, following every symlink. Without interference the trace shows `readlink("/proc/534/fd/3") = "/tmp/benign/app.lock.db"` and then a second `openat` of that path. The descriptor contributes only a string. Once the directory entry behind the descriptor is gone, the string is `<database> (deleted)`. A symlink with that exact name sends SQLite wherever its creator chose.  The other user prepares the directory before the lock user runs. They create a database `cache.lock.db` (`0666`, so the lock user's lock accepts it) with a second hard link `cache.lock.db.keep`, and the symlink `cache.lock.db (deleted) -> /tmp/victim-notes.txt`. The lock user's `os.open` raises an inotify `IN_OPEN` event. The other user unlinks `cache.lock.db` and links `cache.lock.db.keep` back under the same name. The lock user's descriptor still refers to the unlinked entry, so `/proc/self/fd/3` now reads `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)`. `sqlite3.connect` resolves it, follows the symlink and opens the target `O_RDWR|O_CREAT`. None of filelock's checks look at that file. `_open_lock_database` and `_raise_if_wal` inspect descriptor 3. `_raise_if_database_replaced` compares an `lstat` of the lock path with the descriptor's `(st_dev, st_ino)`, which passes because the other user linked the same inode back, and it runs only after `BEGIN`.  The damage comes from the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`. SQLite finds `<target>-journal`, treats it as the rollback journal of an interrupted transaction, and copies its page records into the target before it checks whether the target is a database at all. The journal header supplies the page size and the page count SQLite resizes the file to. Whoever wrote the journal computed the per-page checksum. The content from offset 0 and the final length are therefore the other user's. Strace of the lock user's process (SQLite 3.40.1):  ``` openat("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NONBLOCK|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0600) = 3 readlink("/proc/3819/fd/3", "/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", 4096) = 41 readlink("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", "/tmp/victim-notes.txt", 4096) = 21 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0644) = 4 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal", O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC) = 5 pread64(5, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 516) = 4096 pwrite64(4, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 0) = 4096 unlink("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal") = -1 EPERM            -> "disk I/O error" ```  The redirect itself needs no journal. The constructor's validation connection already makes SQLite open the target with `O_CREAT`. With the symlink pointing at a missing path in the lock user's home, constructing the lock created that file (empty, `0644`, owned by the lock user) and raised nothing. With the symlink pointing at a `0600` WAL-mode SQLite database of the lock user, `write_lock()` returned without error and the database's header bytes 18 and 19 changed from `2 2` to `1 1`. The pragma converted the lock user's database out of WAL mode, and the redirected acquire held its SQLite lock on that database rather than on the lock database.  **Side-file names beside the database.** Two comments record the belief that SQLite names its side files after the descriptor path ([line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), [line 1095](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1095)). The path is not synthetic to SQLite. It derives `<database>-journal`, `<database>-wal` and `<database>-shm` from the resolved real path in the shared directory. `journal_mode=MEMORY` governs only journals SQLite would write, not ones it finds. These variants need no redirect.  *A hot `-journal` makes the lock user unlink a file the journal names; no race.* The other user unlinks the lock user's empty `lock.db`, puts a one-page SQLite database (`0666`) in its place, and writes a 46-byte `lock.db-journal`: a path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. SQLite treats a journal beside a non-empty database as hot (left by an interrupted transaction). The tail names a "super-journal", and recovery ends by unlinking that file. The lock user's next `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` returns without error and the named file is gone (`unlink("/home/victim/private/notes.txt") = 0`, from a `0700` directory of the lock user). The named file must be a non-empty regular file the lock user can read and unlink. A FIFO planted as `lock.db-journal` instead blocks `read_lock(timeout=2)` in SQLite's `open()` of the journal (still blocked when killed after 10 s).  *A re-planted `-wal` puts the holder in WAL mode past `_raise_if_wal`.* `_raise_if_wal` checks header bytes 18 and 19. Whenever a connection takes its first lock, SQLite stats `<db>-wal`, and if that file and the database are both non-empty it opens the WAL whatever the header says. The pragma at line 816 converts such a database and unlinks `-wal` and `-shm`. The `BEGIN` at line 833 is a separate statement that starts unlocked and stats `<db>-wal` again. Re-creating the 32-byte `-wal` in that gap landed on the first attempt in 20 of 20 runs on a 2-CPU machine.  The lock user's `with lock.write_lock():` then holds the `-shm` byte-120 WAL write lock and only SHARED on the database. Once the other user removes the `-wal`, a second process of the lock user gets `read_lock(timeout=1)` granted while the writer is inside its block, with no exception on either side. SQLite also creates `<db>-shm` with the database's permission bits (`0666`) and keeps it mapped into memory. After the other user truncates it, the writer dies with `SIGBUS` (the signal for touching a mapped file region that no longer exists) in `connection.rollback()` during `release()`.  *A `-wal` in a sticky directory makes every acquire raise; no race, no access to the database.* Beside the lock user's own empty `0600` database, a non-empty `<db>-wal` (one byte, any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) is a leftover SQLite tries to delete. In a `1777` directory the lock user cannot unlink another user's file (`unlink(...) = -1 EPERM`), so the pragma fails with `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`. The code in [`_do_acquire_inner`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) translates only "database is locked" into `Timeout`. `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` therefore leaves every `acquire_read()` / `acquire_write()` (and the async variants) within milliseconds, whatever `timeout` or `blocking` says, until the file's owner or root removes it.  *Further effects observed at this commit in a non-sticky directory.* A `0755` script owned by the lock user, renamed to the lock path with a one-record journal beside it, ends up holding the other user's bytes (the acquire raises `file is not a database`). A hard link to the lock user's `0600` `~/.profile` at the lock path does the same in a sticky `/tmp` when `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. When the locking process runs as root, SQLite runs `fchown` on a `-wal` or `-shm` it opens to match the owner of the database, so root's `0600` `service.env` renamed to `app.lock.db-wal` belonged to the other user after root's `read_lock()`.  A journal whose super-journal names the database itself makes SQLite open and close a second descriptor on the database, which drops the process's POSIX locks, so `acquire_read` returns with no lock held in `/proc/locks` and a writer in another process acquires (two journals in a row, one per statement; write locks are not affected). A one-byte `lock.db-wal` plus a `lock.db-shm` on which the other user holds two byte locks makes the acquire take 10 s regardless of `timeout` and raise `locking protocol`, or die with `SIGBUS` if the other user truncates the `-shm`.  **The hard-link route in a directory without the sticky bit.** None of the above occurs on the `_link_beside` branch (macOS, Linux without `/proc`). There SQLite's main file is `.filelock-…/lock.db` in the connecting user's `0700` directory. That protection holds only where no other user can rename the `.filelock-*` entry itself, because `0700` protects the contents, not the entry in the parent. `_link_beside` checks the link once and returns a pathname, and every later use is by that name.  With `/proc` hidden in a `0777` directory, the other user staged a directory holding a hard link `lock.db` to a one-page database and a hot `lock.db-journal`. They held `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE` on the database so the lock user's first statement waited in the busy handler (SQLite's retry loop for a locked database), renamed the lock user's `.filelock-*` directory aside, renamed the staged directory onto its name and rolled back. SQLite got SHARED, found the journal under the swapped name and unlinked the file it named. The lock user's process reported the lock held and exited 0. A polling variant without the write lock also won (in 40 trials the file was gone after 1 to 26 starts of the lock user's program). Under the sticky bit the rename fails with `EPERM`.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.  **`repro`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import shutil import subprocess import sys  as_victim = {"user": "victim", "group": "victim", "extra_groups": []} as_attacker = {"user": "attacker", "group": "attacker", "extra_groups": []}  # set up: the lock database lives in a shared cache directory, 0777 and not sticky shared_dir = "/tmp/shared-cache" lock_db = shared_dir + "/cache.lock.db" shutil.rmtree(shared_dir, ignore_errors=True) os.mkdir(shared_dir) os.chmod(shared_dir, 0o777)  # set up: a private 0600 file of the victim's in sticky /tmp, which the attacker cannot write target = "/tmp/victim-notes.txt" for leftover in (target, target + "-journal"):     if os.path.lexists(leftover):         os.unlink(leftover) original = b"original victim notes
" with open(target, "wb") as notes:     notes.write(original) shutil.chown(target, "victim", "victim") os.chmod(target, 0o600) direct_write = subprocess.run(     [sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; open(sys.argv[1], 'r+b')", target], capture_output=True, text=True, **as_attacker ) print("attacker opening the target for writing:", direct_write.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1]) assert direct_write.returncode != 0  # attack: a hot journal beside the target, and a redirect of the victim's SQLite from the lock database to the target content = "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE VICTIM'S ReadWriteLock
" subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/plant_hot_journal.py", target, content], check=True, **as_attacker) redirect = subprocess.Popen(     [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/redirect_lock_db.py", lock_db, target], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, **as_attacker ) assert redirect.stdout.readline() == "ready
"  # the victim takes its read lock; the attacker races each acquire, so the victim runs up to 20 times for run in range(1, 21):     victim = subprocess.run(         [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_app.py", lock_db], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60, **as_victim     )     with open(target, "rb") as notes:         after = notes.read()     if after != original:         break redirect.kill() redirect.wait()  # check: taking a lock on cache.lock.db must leave the victim's notes alone print(f"victim run {run}: exit status {victim.returncode}:", (victim.stderr.strip() or "no error").splitlines()[-1]) status = os.stat(target) print("target owner, mode, size:", status.st_uid, oct(status.st_mode & 0o7777), status.st_size) print("target before:", original) print("target after: ", after[:60]) print("BUG" if after == content.encode().ljust(4096, b"\0") else "OK") ```  **`repro.d/plant_hot_journal.py`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """The attacker: leave a rollback journal beside TARGET whose one record restores TARGET's first page to CONTENT."""  import os import struct import sys  target, content = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2].encode() journal_path = target + "-journal"  # https://www.sqlite.org/fileformat2.html#the_rollback_journal JOURNAL_MAGIC = bytes.fromhex("d9d505f920a163d7") page_size, sector_size, nonce = 4096, 512, 0x11223344 record_count = 1 pages_after_rollback = 1  # SQLite truncates TARGET to this many pages header = JOURNAL_MAGIC + struct.pack(">IIIII", record_count, nonce, pages_after_rollback, sector_size, page_size)  page_number = 1  # page 1 starts at offset 0 page_image = content.ljust(page_size, b"\0") # SQLite's pager_cksum(): the nonce plus every 200th byte, counting down from page_size - 200 checksum = (nonce + sum(page_image[i] for i in range(page_size - 200, 0, -200))) & 0xFFFFFFFF record = struct.pack(">I", page_number) + page_image + struct.pack(">I", checksum)  with open(journal_path, "wb") as journal:     journal.write(header.ljust(sector_size, b"\0") + record) os.chmod(journal_path, 0o666)  # the victim's SQLite opens a hot journal O_RDWR ```  **`repro.d/redirect_lock_db.py`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """The attacker: make the victim's SQLite, connecting through /proc/self/fd/<n>, open TARGET instead of LOCK_DB."""  import ctypes import os import sys  lock_db, target = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2] spare_name = lock_db + ".keep"  # the attacker creates the lock database, world-writable so that the victim's ReadWriteLock accepts it os.close(os.open(lock_db, os.O_CREAT | os.O_WRONLY)) os.chmod(lock_db, 0o666) os.link(lock_db, spare_name)  # what /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> reads back as once the name the descriptor was opened through is unlinked os.symlink(target, lock_db + " (deleted)")  IN_OPEN = 0x20 libc = ctypes.CDLL(None, use_errno=True) inotify = libc.inotify_init1(0) if libc.inotify_add_watch(inotify, lock_db.encode(), IN_OPEN) < 0:     raise OSError(ctypes.get_errno(), "inotify_add_watch", lock_db) print("ready", flush=True)  while True:     os.read(inotify, 4096)  # the victim's ReadWriteLock has opened the database and is validating its descriptor     os.unlink(lock_db)     os.link(spare_name, lock_db)  # the same inode back at the path, so filelock's later lstat sees no change ```  **`repro.d/victim_app.py`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """The victim: an application that takes its shared read lock once, as in docs/how-to.rst."""  import sys  from filelock import ReadWriteLock  rw = ReadWriteLock(sys.argv[1]) with rw.read_lock(timeout=5):     pass ```  ## Attack sequence  The redirect, with `A` the other local user:  ```mermaid sequenceDiagram     participant A as other local user     participant V as lock user's process (filelock)     participant S as SQLite inside that process     participant K as kernel and filesystem     rect rgb(255, 214, 214)         Note over A,K: filelock 4.0.9 to 4.2.0 on Linux, lock directory 0777 without the sticky bit         A->>K: create cache.lock.db (0666) and a second hard link cache.lock.db.keep         A->>K: symlink On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.  Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes. - Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.  A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. `StrictSoftFileLock` and `AsyncStrictSoftFileLock` check `<path>.filelock` (the coordination directory that holds the lock's state) with one `lstat` call on its name. `lstat` reports what a name is without following a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path). After that check, the code reaches `<path>.filelock/claims` by pathname for every later operation (`mkdir`, scan, publish, link, unlink). `_open_directory` passes `O_NOFOLLOW` (a flag that makes an open fail when the final name is a symbolic link), but the flag covers only the final `claims` component. The kernel follows a symbolic link in any earlier component.  Another local user (the other user below) who can rename `<path>.filelock` exchanges it for a symbolic link after the check. In a shared directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it), any user with write access can do this. Where the shared directory is sticky, such as `/tmp`, only the user who created `<path>.filelock` before the user running the lock (the lock user below) first used it can. The lock user's process (root's, if root takes the lock) then creates a `claims` directory and claim files (the files whose presence says a process wants or holds the lock) inside a directory the other user chooses but only the lock user can write.  When the link points at another strict lock's `.filelock` directory, the stranded claims make that lock time out for every process until an operator finds and force-breaks each one. The `claims` property and `force_break()` resolve the same path with no check at all. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.30.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-SVFEYX89`).  ## Severity  **CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:H, 5.8 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): the swap must land between the `lstat` and the next `mkdir`. The other user does not aim at that window. It flips the name in a loop with `renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE)` (a system call that swaps two names in one step) across repeated acquires, and won after 1 to 31 runs of the lock user's program in the scanner's trials. A sticky directory also requires it to have created `<path>.filelock` first. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own.  `C:L` (low confidentiality impact): through `claims`, one file name per planted link from a directory only the lock user can list. `I:L` (low integrity impact): a directory named `claims` and files with filelock's fixed claim names and contents appear, created with the lock user's privileges, in a directory the other user chooses but cannot write. The process overwrites or truncates nothing that exists. `A:H` (high availability impact): aimed at another strict lock of the lock user, the stranded claims deny that lock to every process until an operator finds and force-breaks each one. Classification from the review: security, conditional on the other user being able to rename the intermediate component. The scanner rated it high (CWE-363).  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other user can rename `<path>.filelock`. In a writable directory without the sticky bit (a `0777` or group-writable project or cache directory), any user with write permission on the directory can, even though the lock user created and owns `<path>.filelock`. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, only the user who created `<path>.filelock` before the lock user's first use can, because that user then owns both the directory and the symbolic link (the planting precondition of GHSA-9c4x-gm8v-wgc4). - The link's target is a directory the lock user can write. The effect that matters is on that directory. An acquire that completes through the link also holds the shared lock with its claims elsewhere, but a user who can rename `<path>.filelock` can defeat that lock's exclusion anyway. - `fs.protected_symlinks=1` (a Linux setting that refuses to follow another user's symbolic link in a world-writable sticky directory) does not interfere. The link is an intermediate path component, not the last one. In the sticky-directory case it also sits in a directory the other user owns. - Missed attempts show up to the lock user as `SoftFileLockProtocolError` or `FileNotFoundError`. The swap therefore works against a lock that a program takes more than once: a periodic job, a worker pool, or a caller that retries or waits with a timeout (each poll of a waiting acquisition is a new attempt). - The two entry points that need no race (`claims` and `force_break()` on a resting symbolic link) depend on the lock user inspecting or recovering the lock. The planted link invites this by making `acquire()` fail with a protocol error. The `force_break()` variant works only when the lock user breaks claims that name a live process on its own host without checking them first, as the recovery loop in `docs/tutorials.rst` does. `docs/how-to.rst` tells the operator to verify that the named owner is gone before breaking. - Platform: POSIX, demonstrated on Linux (tmpfs and overlayfs). Windows has no `dir_fd` (file operations relative to an open directory handle), and on Windows the documented requirement is a lock directory that untrusted users cannot write.  filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit b831496, the check and the first use are adjacent lines of [`StrictSoftFileLock._acquire`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L123-L128). The doorway (the acquire step that scans existing claims and publishes the caller's own) then publishes into it. A symbolic link resting at `<path>.filelock` stops at the first call with "is not a real directory". That answer describes the name at that instant only; nothing carries it forward. With the name exchanged for a link to a directory `T` between the two calls:  - The second call runs `mkdir("<path>.filelock/claims")`, which creates `T/claims` with the lock user's credentials. The `mkdir` succeeds, so `_ensure_protocol_directory` returns without looking at anything. - `_attempt_doorway` then works in `T/claims` for as long as the name still points there. `_read_existing_claims` uses `directory.exists()` and `os.scandir(directory)`. `_publish_record` opens the claim directory by its full path and creates `.intent-v1-<token>.claim.private-v1-<hex>.tmp` and `intent-v1-<token>.claim` (the intent claim, which announces a pending acquire) in it. When its intent wins the scan, `_link_no_replace` adds `held-v1-<token>.claim` (the held claim, which marks the lock as taken). `_open_directory` does pass `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW`, but on `"<path>.filelock/claims"`, so the flag covers `claims` only. - Cleanup resolves the name again. `_unlink_in_directory` opens `<path>.filelock/claims` by path. When the name is back at the real directory by then, the `unlink` gets `ENOENT` (the "no such file" error), which `_unlink_owner_path_result` counts as removed. The claim file stays in `T/claims`.  When `T/claims` already exists, the `mkdir` takes the `FileExistsError` branch, `lstat` sees a real directory, and the same scan and publication run on the existing directory. With `T/claims` holding a file `secret-name.txt` and an old `.held-v1-<hex>.claim.private-v1-<hex>.tmp`, the lock user's process raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError: … claim 'secret-name.txt': unknown claim name or protocol version`. `_reclaim_private_record` unlinks the private-record file. `intent-*.claim` files and a clock-probe file from `_filesystem_now` stay behind.  The window is a few lines of Python between two system calls, but the other user does not aim at it. `renameat2` with `RENAME_EXCHANGE` flips the name in a loop, so each system call of the lock user sees the directory or the link more or less at random. An attempt that sees the link at the `lstat` raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError`. One that sees the directory there and the link at the next `mkdir` is a hit. Four other ways reach the same by-name resolution. The scanner observed each of them at the same commit, with `victim` and `attacker` as separate accounts and default lock options.  The first way strands claims in another strict lock. With the swapped-in link pointing at the coordination directory of a second lock of the lock user (`/home/victim/private/db.lock.filelock`, parent mode `0700`), 200 acquires of the shared lock left 7 to 17 well-formed `intent-v1-*.claim` and `held-v1-*.claim` files in the second lock's `claims`. No process holds that lock, yet `StrictSoftFileLock("/home/victim/private/db.lock", timeout=1)` raises `Timeout` from then on, until an operator force-breaks each stranded claim.  The second way swaps one component lower, at `claims`. The claim scan does not use a descriptor (an open handle that stays bound to one directory whatever its name later points to). `os.scandir(directory)`, the record reads, `_reclaim_private_record` (called with its descriptor slot set to `None`) and the clock probe in `_filesystem_now` (`os.open(directory / name, O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW)` followed by `probe.unlink()`) all go by pathname. For a sticky directory, the other user needs to have created `<path>.filelock` first. It then puts a real `claims` directory (mode `1777`) in it with one empty file named `.held-v1-<32 zeros>.claim.private-v1-<32 zeros>.tmp`, so that every scan calls the probe, and exchanges `claims` with a link in a loop. The probe open went through the link, and the pathname `unlink` ran after `claims` was a directory again and got `ENOENT`. A swap at this level does not affect publication or release, because there `_open_directory`'s `O_NOFOLLOW` does cover `claims`.  The third way is `claims` with no race. The property calls `_read_existing_claims` on an instance that did not go through `_acquire`, and `directory.exists()` and `os.scandir(directory)` both follow a link. After the other user runs `mkdir /tmp/work.lock.filelock; ln -s /home/victim/private /tmp/work.lock.filelock/claims`, `acquire()` refuses with "is not a real directory". That names the first non-hidden entry, in sort order, of a directory the other user cannot list. A missing or empty target returns `()`, a non-directory gives "Not a directory" and an unreadable directory "Permission denied", so the call also tells those apart.  The fourth way is `force_break()` with no race. The first holder's `release()` later finds its claims gone, counts `ENOENT` as removed and returns without error. Only a directory named `claims` below the link's target is reachable, so the targets are other strict locks, not arbitrary files.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-SVFEYX89`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The other user chooses the location only. filelock fixes the directory name, and the files contain filelock's own claim record (magic, token, PID, host name, start token). The process overwrites or truncates nothing that exists. This amounts to directory and file creation outside the lock's directory with the lock user's privileges, not a write of chosen data.  Where the chosen directory already has a `claims` subdirectory, the lock user's process also scans it, unlinks entries named like stale private records, and raises an error that quotes the first other file name in it. Aimed at another strict lock's `.filelock` directory, the stranded claims deny that lock to every process until an operator finds and `force_break()`s each one. The `force_break()` variant puts two processes inside a different strict lock's critical section, one the other user can neither list nor write, with neither told. Here the link sits one component above the final one, the other user swaps it in after the check that refuses it, and it chooses only the parent directory.  ## Workarounds  Keep strict locks in a directory no other user can write. In a sticky shared directory, create `<path>.filelock` as the service user before any other account can, and check its owner before first use. Do not run the recovery loop from `docs/tutorials.rst` on a lock in a shared directory without first verifying, as `docs/how-to.rst` says, that the owner named in each claim is gone. Treat an unexpected `SoftFileLockProtocolError` that quotes an unknown claim name as a sign that `claims` may point elsewhere. Keep the exception text of `claims` out of logs other accounts can read. ### Summary  `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` resolve the lock path with `pathlib.Path.resolve()` and pass it to `sqlite3.connect()` without refusing a symlink. A local user who can create names in the lock's directory, such as `/tmp` or a shared cache, can plant a symlink at the lock path and make the victim's process create, lock, or write the file it points to, or break mutual exclusion between the victim's own processes.  ### Details  `ReadWriteLock.__init__` stores `pathlib.Path(lock_file).resolve()`, which follows a final symlink, and every connection opens that path through `sqlite3.connect()` with no `O_NOFOLLOW` or regular-file check. SQLite's own VFS also resolves the final symlink in user space, so `fs.protected_symlinks` and the sticky bit do not help: the kernel never sees a symlink to refuse. The other lock classes do not follow a final symlink: `FileLock` opens with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and `SoftReadWriteLock` coordinates through `<path>.rw/`.  ### Proof of concept  On Linux, with the victim and attacker as different users and `/shared` mode 1777 with `fs.protected_symlinks=1`:  1. The attacker runs `ln -s /home/victim/private/pwned.flag /shared/app.rwlock.db`. 2. The victim constructs `ReadWriteLock("/shared/app.rwlock.db")`. A plain `os.open(..., O_NOFOLLOW)` on the same path fails, but the lock creates `/home/victim/private/pwned.flag`, owned by the victim, inside a directory the attacker cannot write. 3. With `/shared/cache.rwlock.db -> /shared/a.db`, one victim process holds the write lock. The attacker repoints the link to `/shared/b.db`, and a second victim process acquires the write lock while the first still holds it.  The same behavior reproduces on macOS, on Windows 11, and through `AsyncReadWriteLock`.  ### Impact  A local attacker with write access to the lock directory can make the victim create empty files it owns at paths the attacker cannot write, make the victim hold a SQLite lock on another application's database so that application gets `database is locked`, and give two victim processes the write lock at once, letting them corrupt the resource the lock protects.  ### Workarounds  Keep `ReadWriteLock` paths in directories that only trusted users can write.

filelock on Windows ignores the `mode` argument. `FileLock(path, mode=0o600)` creates the same file as `FileLock(path)`: one with no security descriptor of its own (the Windows record that says who may access a file). Its access list, or ACL, is whatever the lock directory hands down to new files. filelock creates the `ReadWriteLock` database, which it asks to be `0o600`, the same way. In a directory whose inheritable ACL grants other local accounts access to new files, those accounts can open the lock file or database. They can take the byte-range lock (a lock on a span of bytes in a file) once the owner releases it and keep the owner's later `acquire()` calls waiting or timing out. They can read holder metadata an `on_acquired` hook left in a `preserve_lock_file=True` file. Where the directory hands down modify access, they can write to both files.  `lock.mode` still reports `0o600`. The documentation neither promises an ACL on Windows nor says that Windows drops the mode. On Unix the same mode keeps other accounts out. Mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol holds on either platform. Affected versions are filelock 3.10.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows.  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:  - `ANT-2026-0KEO0DDO` [medium, CWE-732]: WindowsFileLock ignores mode; 0o600 lock files inherit the directory ACL.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L` scores 5.3 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): no race. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the lock file (holder metadata) and the lock database are readable where `0o600` was meant to keep them private. `I:L` (partial integrity impact): in the directory layout the maintainers tested, the other account can also write both files, which lets it corrupt the lock's own state but nothing the lock protects. `A:L` (partial availability impact): the other account can hold the byte-range lock and make the owner wait or time out. `S:U` (scope unchanged).  Classification from the review: **Windows permission failure with security impact only where callers rely on `mode=0o600` across accounts**. The review had marked it an unconfirmed Windows claim, since the scanner traced stand-in Win32 calls on Linux. The scanner rated this medium; the maintainers keep medium.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The affected classes are `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Windows (`WindowsFileLock`), and the SQLite database of `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`. Examples are a service's data directory readable by `Users`, or any directory with `(OI)(CI)` entries (entries that new files and sub-directories inherit) for another account. A directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts, such as one inside a user profile, hides the problem. - The other account must open the file. According to the `LockFileEx` documentation, read access is enough to take the byte-range lock, so it can hold the lock whenever the owner does not. The lock file exists while the owner holds the lock, and stays after release with `preserve_lock_file=True`. The `ReadWriteLock` database is not unlinked at any point. - Unix is not affected, because `UnixFileLock` creates the file with the mode and repeats it with `fchmod`. Mutual exclusion between cooperating processes is not affected.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_open_non_reparse_fd` reduces the mode to one `read_only` bit](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L252-L253). That bit is false for every accepted mode, because [`_check_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L526) rejects any mode without owner read and write, and an unset mode becomes `0o666`. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1086) passes `0o600` through the same function on Windows.  ## Introduced  [d0061e4](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d0061e4643df) "added multiuser support and associated tests" ([#192](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/192), 2023-03-15), first tag 3.10.0 (verified), added the `mode` parameter and on Windows handed it to `os.open`, which applies only the read-only attribute. The Windows backend has applied no more of the mode than that at any version, so this is a long-standing gap rather than a regression.  ## Mechanism  `_open_non_reparse_fd(path, mode)` computes `read_only = not mode & _OWNER_WRITE` and calls `_nt_open(path, read_only=read_only)`. `_nt_open` fills an `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` with the NT path and `OBJ_CASE_INSENSITIVE` and leaves `SecurityDescriptor` NULL. It then calls `NtCreateFile` with `FILE_OPEN_IF` and `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL` (or `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY` when `read_only`, which no accepted mode produces). Nothing consults the group and other bits. Per the `NtCreateFile` and `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` documentation, a NULL descriptor gives the new file default security, which on NTFS is the set of inheritable entries of the parent directory. A lock file created with `mode=0o600` in a directory that hands down read access to `Users` is therefore readable by `Users`.  Nothing tells the caller. The constructor validates the mode, `lock.mode` returns `0o600`, and `has_explicit_mode` is `True`. `docs/concepts.rst` says "filelock creates the file with it" and that "`0o600` and `0o700` keep other UIDs out", with no Windows caveat. Maintainer triage: the stand-in reproducer prints `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 release image.  Maintainer verification on Windows 11 with two local accounts: a script creates `private.lock` with `FileLock(mode=0o600, preserve_lock_file=True)`, `default.lock` without a mode, and a `ReadWriteLock` database `lock.db` as the first account, in a directory granted `(OI)(CI)(M)` to a second account that is a member of `Users`. It then opens each file under the second account's logon token with `LogonUserW` and `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser`. On 4.2.0 the second account could open `private.lock` and `lock.db` for both read and write, the same as `default.lock`, and `icacls` listed only inherited `(I)` entries on all three. This confirms the claim the review had marked unconfirmed.  ## Impact  A program that passes `mode=0o600` so that other accounts cannot open its lock file gets no such restriction on Windows. In a directory that hands down read access, another account can hold the lock and make the owner wait or time out, and read holder metadata in a preserved lock file. Where the directory hands down modify access, as in the maintainers' test, it can also write the lock file and the `ReadWriteLock` database. With the mode honoured, as on Unix, a user without write access to the directory can do none of this. The exposure ends there: the effect reaches only the lock file or lock database, and mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol still holds.  ## Workarounds  - On Windows, keep lock files and `ReadWriteLock` databases in a directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts (inside the user profile, or a directory with inheritance disabled and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted), rather than relying on `mode`. - After creating a lock file with `preserve_lock_file=True` or a `ReadWriteLock` database, set its ACL yourself, for example `icacls <file> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:F" "SYSTEM:F" "Administrators:F"`; a file that exists keeps its ACL on later opens. - Do not store anything confidential in the lock file through `on_acquired` on Windows.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. `UnixFileLock`, the backend of `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix, empties whatever regular file it finds at the lock path once it holds the `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file). With an explicit `mode` it also chmods that file (sets its permission bits), whether or not this acquire created it. Another local user who can rename or hard-link one of the files of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the lock path gets that file truncated by the lock user's next `acquire()`. A hard link is a second name for the same file. With a mode such as `0o666` the file, still owned by the lock user, also becomes readable and writable by that other user. The other user can then read and alter everything the lock user writes to it afterwards.  `O_NOFOLLOW`, the defence added for the symlink variant (CVE-2025-68146), does not see a renamed file or a hard link. The rename route needs the file's directory to be writable without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The hard-link route into a sticky directory such as `/tmp` needs `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`, a Linux kernel setting. Affected versions are every filelock release up to and including 4.2.0 (the truncation is as old as the project; the chmod since 3.10.2).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:  - `ANT-2026-KO573NWI` [high, CWE-706]: UnixFileLock truncates and chmods victim files renamed onto the lock path.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N` scores 6.1 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): one rename or link, then wait for the lock user's next acquire; no race. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the lock user's own process truncates a file it did not mean to touch, including content behind a second name the other user could neither modify nor delete. With a permissive explicit `mode` the other user can then write to it. If that file is one the lock user later executes or trusts, that is code execution as the lock user. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the old content is gone before the other user can read anything, but what the lock user writes afterwards through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file) it still holds is readable. `A:N` (no availability impact). `S:U` (scope unchanged).  Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on another user controlling names in a non-sticky directory on the lock's filesystem (or on `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`). The scanner rated this high. The maintainers score it medium because the reachable targets depend on the directory layout and kernel settings described below.  ## Scope and preconditions  - Lock classes: `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix (`UnixFileLock`). `SoftFileLock` applies an explicit mode only to a file it created with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and does not truncate an existing file. `WindowsFileLock` has not truncated at any version. - The other user must put a regular file of the lock user at the lock path before the lock user's next acquire, while the lock file does not exist yet. That is the case on first use, after a reboot, after a `/tmp` cleaner, or after a release with the default `preserve_lock_file=False`, which unlinks the file. The scanner checked three ways at the scanned commit, with default kernel settings unless stated:   - rename inside a directory without the sticky bit (a group-writable project or cache directory, a root-created `0777` directory);   - rename from such a directory into a sticky one (`1777`) on the same filesystem. The sticky bit only protects entries that already exist, so the move succeeds while the lock path is free. Once the lock user's lock file exists there, the same move fails with `EPERM`;   - `link(2)` into a sticky directory. This needs a system that lets a user hard-link a file it cannot write, which on Linux means `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. Mainstream distributions set 1, which refuses the link. The scanner did not test macOS or the BSDs. - What the lock user loses: with the default `FileLock(path)` the lock truncates the file, which keeps its mode. With an explicit `mode` (a lock shared between users needs `0o666` or `0o660`, because `UnixFileLock` opens the file read-write), the lock also chmods the file to that mode. `_apply_explicit_mode` suppresses `PermissionError` only for files the lock user does not own. The lock user owns its own files, so the `fchmod` succeeds. - Trust boundary: the protection against another local user holds only when no other user can rename entries in the lock's directory or, for the rename-into-sticky route, in any directory on the same filesystem that holds a file of the lock user. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against. - Not affected: a symlink (a file that points at another path) at the lock path, because `O_NOFOLLOW` makes the open fail with `ELOOP`; mutual exclusion between cooperating processes.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L144-L163), whose [`os.ftruncate` and `_apply_explicit_mode` calls](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L150-L154) have only the `st_nlink != 0` guard (the file still has at least one name); [`_apply_explicit_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L165-L168); [`_open_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L95-L121), which learns from its `O_EXCL` create whether this attempt made the file but hands that flag only to the `ENOSYS` fallback.  ## Introduced  The truncation of whatever is at the lock path dates from the initial commit ([2157efb](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/2157efb8b57666699fcf15bf03c3771c1571279c), which opened with `O_TRUNC`). With the lock user's file renamed to the lock path that fails with `FileExistsError`. The second `os.open(path, O_RDWR | O_NOFOLLOW)` succeeds, because the entry is a regular file the lock user owns, and returns `created = False`. `_acquire_native` passes `created` only to the `ENOSYS` branch. No process holds a `flock` on the renamed file, so `_lock_fd_nonblocking(fd)` succeeds at once and `_finalize_locked_fd(fd)` runs: `os.fstat`, `st_nlink != 0`, `os.ftruncate(fd, 0)`, then `os.fchmod(fd, mode)` when the lock has an explicit mode. There is no race: the other user renames or links once and waits for the next acquire. `AsyncUnixFileLock` inherits `_finalize_locked_fd` unchanged. With an explicit permissive `mode`, the other user can read and modify everything the lock user writes afterwards, while the file still belongs to the lock user. The other user can rename the file back to its old name after the acquire. It stays there with the lock's mode, and the lock user's next acquire creates a fresh lock file.  Somebody who may rename a single-name file may also unlink it, so losing such a file under its name is not new. What the lock adds are two operations on the inode that the other user cannot perform, `ftruncate` and `fchmod`, run with the lock user's privileges. Those matter for a descriptor the lock user still holds, for a second name of the file, and for programs that trust the file's ownership. The other user does not choose the mode, and the lock user writes no bytes the other user chose. Mutual exclusion is not affected.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the lock file in a directory no other account can write, or in a sticky directory on a filesystem where no directory holding the lock user's files is writable by others. On Linux keep `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (the default on mainstream distributions), which closes the hard-link route. - Do not pass a permissive explicit `mode` (`0o666`, `0o660`, `0o644`) unless accounts share the lock; without a mode the exposure is the truncation only. - Keep the lock file in place (`preserve_lock_file=True`). This goes beyond what holding the lock gives that user, because a held lock ends in `Timeout` when the caller's timeout runs out, and this does not. With the looping-page layout the acquiring thread spins at 100% of one CPU on a free lock, `Timeout` is not raised, Ctrl-C does not interrupt it, and only killing the process ends it. It is a denial of service of the lock user's process only: it reads nothing and corrupts nothing, and in the long-row case the lock is still granted afterwards.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. - Do not give the lock a database another account may write. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. A lock shared between accounts through a `0666` database stays reachable even in `/tmp`. - If a stall or hang appears, the file at the lock path is the cause; replacing it with an empty file restores the lock.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. The stale-lock break shared by `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` (and their async variants, and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS`, the "not implemented" error) recognises the marker it judged stale by two values. The marker is the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock. The values are its inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) and its modification time (mtime) not being newer. The check runs after the contender has already closed the marker, so nothing keeps the inode allocated.  On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file (ext4, xfs, overlayfs on them) the next holder's marker can carry that number. A contender still between its read and its break then renames and unlinks the live marker. Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), forces this at will. It plants a marker with a stale owner record and a modification time in the future and unlinks it as soon as a contender has read it. Two processes of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then hold the same default-configured lock at once, and nothing raises or logs. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.22.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-KIIS96IX`).  ## Severity  **CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race, though one the other user starts, lengthens (by making the lock user's `/proc` read slow) and retries at every release. The scanner measured 10 to 26 overlaps per 20-second run. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.  Classification from the review: security, conditional on a sticky shared directory, ext4-style inode reuse and at least two contenders of the lock user. Our review verified it across UIDs (a UID is a user account's numeric id): the other user as uid 1001, the lock user's processes as uid 1000, BUG on 4.2.0 over ext4. The scanner rated it high (CWE-367).  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned `1777` directory such as `/tmp` or `/var/tmp` is enough. It creates, `utime`s (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. The sticky bit stops it removing the lock user's marker (checked: `EPERM`, operation not permitted), so the lock user's own stale break does the deletion. - The directory is on a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file. ext4 does (six create/unlink rounds returned one number six times, in the image's overlayfs `/tmp` and on a loop-mounted ext4), and xfs does. tmpfs returned six increasing numbers and the same run there gave no overlap, and btrfs does not hand a freed number back. - The lock user has at least two processes contending for the lock, and the displaced holder is still inside when the next contender polls (the breaker itself comes back one `poll_interval`, 50 ms by default, later). - The lock is `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` or `SoftFileLease` (or async forms). That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. ".encode()  # To compare start tokens a contender reads /proc/<pid>/stat, and the kernel walks every thread of that process: # with 8000 threads that is about 1 ms between the contender reading the marker and breaking it. threading.stack_size(64 * 1024) for _ in range(8000):     threading.Thread(target=threading.Event().wait, daemon=True).start() print("ready", flush=True)  while True:     # plant the stale marker whenever the lock path is free     try:         fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)     except FileExistsError:         time.sleep(0.0002)         continue     os.write(fd, stale_marker)     os.utime(fd, (marker_mtime, marker_mtime))  # a file's owner may give it any modification time     os.close(fd)      # once a contender has read it, unlink it: its inode number is free again for the next holder's marker     inotify = libc.inotify_init()     libc.inotify_add_watch(inotify, lock_path.encode(), IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE)     os.read(inotify, 4096)     os.unlink(lock_path)     os.close(inotify)      # creating anything before the next holder does would take that inode number away from it     while not os.path.lexists(lock_path):         time.sleep(0.0002) ```  **`repro.d/victim_job.py`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import random import sys import time  from filelock import SoftFileLock  lock_path, run_seconds = sys.argv[1], float(sys.argv[2])  lock = SoftFileLock(lock_path) stop_at = time.monotonic() + run_seconds while time.monotonic() < stop_at:     with lock:         entered = time.monotonic()         time.sleep(random.uniform(0.05, 0.15))  # the work the lock protects         print(entered, time.monotonic(), lock.is_locked, flush=True) ```  ## Beside them runs an `attacker` process (uid 1001) with 8000 idle threads that plants its marker whenever the path is free, waits for `IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE`, unlinks it and waits for the next `victim` marker. The control (markers dated 2000) prints `191 holds by 6 victim jobs, two jobs inside the lock at once: 0 times`. The disturbed run (dated 2100) prints `196 holds, two jobs inside the lock at once: 15 times`, for example `job3 inside 130.436-130.530, job5 inside 130.444-130.521`, with `stale-break files left in /tmp/shared-locks: []`. Six runs gave between 11 and 24 overlaps, 0 in each control, every `with` block ending without error with `is_locked == True`.  An `strace` of a landed round shows A's `close(4</tmp/app.lock>(deleted))`, B's `openat(O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL|...)` with `st_ino=296421`, and A's `lstat`, `rename`, `lstat`, `unlink` all on 296421, followed by B's `write(4</tmp/app.lock.break.32232.7d9f...>(deleted), ...)` and A's own create 53 ms later.  Our review ran the reproducer over a loop-mounted ext4 `/tmp` inside the container (the host's btrfs does not reuse a number). Result: BUG on 4.2.0 in 43 s, with the other user as uid 1001 against the lock user's processes as uid 1000; it created and unlinked only its own file in a root-owned `1777` directory. On btrfs the same run is OK, so the condition is the filesystem's inode allocation. On the head of #843 the run was OK with 0 overlaps in 193 holds.  ## Impact  A local user who can create files in the lock's directory puts two processes of another user inside the same default-configured `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` or `SoftFileLease` at once, with no exception, no `lifetime`, no lease expiry and no `break_lock()` involved. Two holders then write the data the lock protects. `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` holders learn nothing. A displaced `SoftFileLease` holder got `compromise.reason == "owner-changed"` at its first heartbeat (the periodic refresh a lease holder runs) when the second holder's marker was still at the path, and `None` after 13 s when the second holder had already released.  It is a race, but the other user controls the start and the length of the window, and each failed attempt costs the lock user's processes one poll. Under the same interference with two processes of the lock user and 20 ms critical sections, 26 of 110 holds in 60 s found their own marker unlinked (`st_nlink == 0`, no name left for the file) while inside, without two holds overlapping. Not affected: tmpfs and btrfs, a lock with a single contender, `StrictSoftFileLock`.  ## Workarounds  Keep soft locks in a directory other users cannot create files in (a `0700` directory of the lock's user) rather than a shared sticky directory, or place the lock directory on tmpfs, which does not reuse inode numbers. Where the native `FileLock` works (local ext4 with `flock`), prefer it over `SoftFileLock`. `StrictSoftFileLock` is not affected.  ## Patched version  4.2.1.  Fix: https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/843  ## Credits  Reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner (automated analysis), 15 October 2026; reviewed by the maintainers.  - 2026-10-15 23:08 UTC: report received (finding `ANT-2026-KIIS96IX`, scanned commit b831496b0273) - 2026-10-16 01:42 UTC: fix PR #843 opened - 2026-10-16 05:38 UTC: draft advisory created

`StrictSoftFileLock` and `AsyncStrictSoftFileLock` apply the caller's `mode` to the sentinel (the lock file at `<path>`) and to both claim files (the files whose presence says a process wants or holds the lock). They create the two directories that hold the claims, `<path>.filelock` and `<path>.filelock/claims`, with a bare `mkdir()`. That gives `0o777` filtered through the umask (a per-process mask that removes permission bits from new files and directories) or, under a parent with a default ACL (an access control list on a directory that sets the permissions of entries created inside it), through that ACL.  A hold consists of two claim names in that directory, which has no sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it). When the environment leaves another local user (the other user below) a write bit on the directory, that user can unlink the holder's `0600` claims. Three settings do this: umask `000` in a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, umask `002` with the other user in the directory's group, or a default ACL on the lock's parent that grants the group write (the kernel then ignores the umask). After the unlink, the next contender of the holder's account finds the directory empty and enters. The first holder keeps reporting `is_locked == True` and later releases with no error. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.30.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-AD6SUOON`).  ## Severity  **CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L, 5.3 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): the holder must pass a restrictive `mode` while its umask or the parent's default ACL leaves the other user a write bit on new directories, and a contender of the holder's account must ask for the lock after the claims are gone. With the common umask `022` and no default ACL the directories are `0755`, and the kernel refuses the other user's unlink. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the holder's processes act on their own.  `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the `0600` claim files stay unreadable. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders then write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:L` (low availability impact): the same write access lets the other user create names in `claims`, and an empty file named `held-v1-<32 zeros>.claim` makes the next `acquire()` raise `SoftFileLockProtocolError` ("malformed claim record") until someone removes it. Classification from the review: security, conditional on a lax umask or a permissive default ACL. The scanner rated it high (CWE-732).  ## Scope and preconditions  - The holder passes a restrictive `mode` such as `0o600`. Without one, the umask decides the permissions by documented design (the "File permissions and mode" section of `docs/concepts.rst` defines `mode` only for the lock file). Umask `000` with the default mode gives the same two-holder result but is outside this finding. - The holder's environment leaves the other user a write bit on new directories. The scanner measured three ways, with `mode=0o600` and the other user a member of group `team`:    | lock's parent directory | holder's umask | `<path>.filelock` and `claims/` | who can unlink the claims |   |---|---|---|---|   | `1777`, like `/tmp` | `000` | `0777` | any other local user |   | `root:team`, `3775` (setgid, so new entries inherit the group, and sticky) | `002` | `2775` | any member of `team` |   | `root:team`, `1770`, default ACL `group:team:rwx` (`setfacl -d -m g:team:rwx`) | `077` | `0770` | any member of `team` |   | `root:team`, `3775`, no ACL | `022` | `2755` | no one; the second process times out |    The default-ACL row is the strongest. A holder with a private umask and `mode=0o600` still gets group-writable claim directories. The lock file in that row is `0600`, because its mode reaches `os.open` and masks the inherited ACL. - A contender that may enter asks for the lock: another process of the holder's account, or root. Nothing needs planting beforehand. The holder creates and owns the whole tree, so the existing-directory branch of `_ensure_protocol_directory` (the subject of GHSA-9c4x-gm8v-wgc4) plays no part. - Directories that an affected release already created keep their mode. A `0777` `<path>.filelock` from an earlier run stays writable by other users after an upgrade, because filelock does not remove these directories. Upgraders should `chmod` or remove existing `<path>.filelock` trees (see Workarounds). - The other lock classes do not have this gap in the same setting. With umask `000` and `mode=0o600`, `FileLock` and `SoftFileLock` create one `0600` file and nothing else, and `SoftReadWriteLock` creates its directories `0700` under any umask. Platform: POSIX permission semantics; demonstrated on Linux.  filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock's user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit b831496, the bare `mkdir()` sits in [`_ensure_protocol_directory`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L996-L998). [`StrictSoftFileLock._acquire`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L127-L133) calls it for both levels without a mode.
